#5624. Every Car Brand That's Made A V10-Powered Sedan

With downsizing being a priority today, thanks chiefly to ever-stricter emissions regulations, a good number of supercars are being sold with six-cylinder engines. In fact, you could even argue that some four-cylinder cars could qualify as supercars today. However, less than a decade earlier, we had a trio of V10-powered sedans sitting in mainstream automaker showrooms — crazy, yet that was the reality of the '00s super-sedan market. BMW dropped a 5.0-liter V10 mill into an otherwise fairly regular-looking 5 Series, Audi furnished its S- and RS-badged sedans with a 5.2-liter lump, and Volkswagen went so far as to develop a diesel-powered V10 for its Bentley-based luxobarge that hardly anyone even remembers existed.

This article shines a light on those fascinating 10-cylinder sedans, zeroing in on the prices, performance specs, and general absurdity each brought to the table. We'll also take a look at how much each example commands today, and what litany of issues typically drain the wallet of anyone foolish enough to take one on. While those models are listed below in chronological order of release, we've also included a brief look at a pair of show-stopping V10-powered sedan concepts that sadly never saw the light of day. One was silenced by a shift in direction, while another found itself permanently postponed by the hands of the '08 financial crisis.

The Volkswagen Phaeton was the first 10-cylinder sedan to break onto the market. It arrived in 2003, designed to elevate Volkswagen's position in the car industry, and Ferdinand Piëch and his team equipped it with all the vital tools to do so. Air suspension, immensely comfortable leather seats, a ridiculously complex A/C system, and a whole host of cool engine options.

The base model came with Volkswagen's weird VR6, which sounds ace and delivers a respectable punch of power — as does the optional 4.2-liter V8. A 3.0-liter direct-injection turbodiesel (TDI) was available in other markets, but for the big spenders, Volkswagen offered both a 6.0-liter W12 and a 4.9-liter V10 TDI. The latter produced 313 horsepower alongside 553 pound-feet of torque – ample for a German luxury sedan at the time.

It wasn't an option that made it to the U.S. market. Instead, Americans received the V8 and W12. Across the pond in the U.K., though, the V10 Phaeton went on sale in early 2003 with a sticker of £57,840, or the equivalent of $95,574 back then. Adjusted for inflation, that comes out to about $175,000 today. Depreciation has really played its part with this forgotten flagship, though, and as a result, prices rarely top £10,000 ($13,480) today. Meanwhile, its W12-powered counterparts regularly trade hands for around $15,000 to $20,000 in the U.S., depending on mileage.

As for what to watch out for, the consensus is just about everything. There was little room in the engine bay, so owners detail that some jobs — like turbocharger replacement — are an engine-out ordeal. That makes work both labor-intensive and not DIY-friendly, and big bills make what is essentially a fancy Passat quite difficult to justify.

It was the E60-generation M5 that next appeared on the 10-cylinder sedan scene, debuting as a 2005 model year. Unlike the Phaeton, which was sold as a comfort-first luxury car, the E60 M5 was first and foremost a performance car. It famously takes power from the naturally aspirated S85 5.0-liter V10, which delivers 500 hp alongside 384 lb-ft of torque. A high compression ratio of 12:1 ensured the M5 meets its 100-hp-per-liter target, and it revs all the way to 8,250 rpm, too. The brilliance of this design was rewarded with the coveted International Engine of the Year Award in both '05 and '06, and it's an engine that still attracts much enthusiast attention 20-plus years later.

When new, buyers would have had to fork out $84,895 for one of these V10-powered super-sedans, and while they have indeed depreciated quite heavily over the last two decades, prices are once again on the move. Classic.com shows $25,555 as the average price paid for SMG-equipped examples, while six-speed manual cars command a significant premium at $45,127. That premium comes down to collectors cherishing the stick-shift involvement, but also ostensibly to the fact that SMG transmissions are so troublesome and expensive to repair — hydraulic pump failures are regular and can easily set owners back thousands of dollars to correct. Aside from SMG woes, the V10 itself is particularly trouble-prone, with its oil pump, throttle body actuators, and rod bearings being known weak spots.

Volkswagen and BMW put their V10 engines into multiple cars, but only ever into a single sedan. Audi outdid them both combined, placing V10s under the hood of C6-generation S6 and RS6 models, in addition to the D3-era S8. The V10-powered S6 arrived in the U.S. as a 2007 model year, as did the S8, while the C6 RS6 sadly avoided the U.S. market altogether.

In these S6 and S8 sedans, torque sat at 398 lb-ft, although the S8 delivered a touch more horsepower: 450 hp compared to the S6's 435. However, when it comes to sheer performance, the forbidden-fruit RS model is the real star of the show. While the S-badged cars featured a naturally aspirated 5.2-liter V10, the RS6 used a 5.0-liter V10 aided by a pair of turbochargers. At the time of its 2008 model-year debut, it was the most powerful production Audi car of all time, kicking out 579 hp and 479 lb-ft.

When shiny and new, buyers were paying £76,160 for an RS6 Sedan, or the equivalent of about $150,000 back then, which would amount to $239,440 today. We drove the latest RS6 Avant, which cost $122,995, so perhaps the C6-era car was a little expensive, but applying financial logic to a twin-turbocharged 10-cylinder probably isn't the best way to look at such a car.

Like the others, these cars have depreciated massively. A simple oil pump seal often necessitates a multi-thousand-dollar engine-out job on the RS6, and that pretty much sets the precedent for any 10-cylinder sedan ownership experience. Still, the fact that used U.S.-market S6 and S8 models can be secured for below $10,000 with reasonable mileage today at least leaves the deep-pocketed among us plenty of cash left over for maintenance.

That concludes our list of V10-powered sedans that made production, and it might seem remarkable that $25,000 is enough to find yourself in a seat in any of them. What's interesting, though, is that a different pair of automakers also looked to produce their own 10-cylinder sedans in the '00s, but sadly never made it all the way.

First up was Ford. The Blue Oval brand released its startling 427 Concept in 2003, and it was designed to recapture the glory of America's traditional and luxurious four-door sedan. Motivating the sharp concept was a modular V10, which boasted a full 427 cubic inches of displacement plus 590 hp and 509 lb-ft of torque — all of which was directed toward the rear wheels. In the end, it remained just a concept, as Ford instead shifted its attention toward other performance models, such as the 2005 Ford GT and the S-197 Mustang.

The other concept worth shining a light on is the 2008 Lamborghini Estoque. It was sort of the Urus before the Urus, but it wasn't an SUV but rather a Lamborghini designed around daily life — think commutes and school drop-offs, rather than cross-country road trips and tire-shredding track days. It was set to be powered by a variant of the Gallardo V10. Buyers could have expected somewhere in the region of 500 horsepower, but it was never to be. With the global recession underway, and Lamborghini ready to explore a more practical model, the Estoque was no longer the flavor of the month. Instead, the Urus would have its day, but we can still reminisce about what could have been.

#5623. DC Gym Shooter Kills His Building Manager After HOA Dispute Over Mold Issues

A Washington, DC, doctor who had been locked in a legal battle with his homeowners association over mold problems fatally shot the manager of his condominium during a shooting spree on Thursday, police said.

The fatal shooting incident was reported around 8 a.m. in the Logan Circle neighborhood in Northwest DC, about a mile from the White House, drawing dozens of heavily armed police officers to the area.

Matt Wade Lambert, 55, a physician living in a penthouse apartment at the Metropole Condos building on 15th Street Northwest, was identified by the authorities as the shooter who killed one and injured four others before taking his own life.

Lambert was suspected of going down to the luxury VIDA Fitness center housed inside the building, locating the building manager, identified las 46-year-old James Stuart, next to the treadmills and shooting him with a handgun from a point-blank range, DC Councilmember Brooke Pinto told reporters, according to WUSA9.

"Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," gymgoer James Spellman told The Associated Press. "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck."

Dozens of people were in the middle of their morning workout in the gym at the time of the deadly attack, which triggered an evacuation and an order to shelter in place in the area.

While law enforcement officials have not revealed an official motive for the shooting, Pinto said that the building manager was "targeted" by the suspect.

During a press conference Thursday evening, Interim DC Police Chief Jeff Carroll said that Lambert then ran out of the gym, went up to his seventh-floor patio and opened fire from a rifle, striking two men and two women who were downstairs. Earlier reports said three of them were construction workers.

One of the victims was hospitalized in critical condition and three others sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Lambert eventually barricaded himself inside his condo at Metropole Circle and was on the phone with police negotiators when he ended his own life with a shotgun blast.

When officers breached the door, they found all three firearms used during the shootings, along with containers of flammable liquid.

DC Mayor Muriel Bowser described the incident as a "senseless act of gun violence."

Court records reviewed by Realtor.com® indicate that Lambert had been in a long-standing feud with his condo’s management and filed a lawsuit in March 2025. In it he claimed that he had not been able to live in his seventh-floor penthouse since Nov. 11, 2024, because of mold, moisture, foul odor, and related damage.

Lambert argued in the 12-page complaint that the problems in his unit were caused by repairs to the building’s facade that had been performed by a contractor, for which he paid over $15,000 as part of a special assessment.

According to the filing, Lambert had incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the HOA's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation."

A mediation in the case had been scheduled for March 2027.

Attorney Joel Braithewaite, who represented Lambert in the case, told NBC News that he spoke with him just yesterday or the day before and said that the 55-year-old was "in a good place" and about to start a new job on Monday.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5622. $3.4 Billion — Anthropic Order for Gas Power Plants!

Wow, this is a nasty, dirty, polluting stunner I didn’t see until just now.

Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, has reportedly signed a $3.4 billion contract to buy gas-fired engines (power plants) from OnePWR Solutions, a Texas-based energy company. These gas power plants would be able to provide Anthropic’s AI data centers with an enormous amount of off-grid electricity — with the real cost being an enormous amount of air pollution and global warming emissions.

If you thought Anthropic was supposed to be “the good guy” in the AI industry, perhaps think again.

The Financial Times, which broke the news on this, says that this is the “largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab.” It’s this line from Futurism that really sums up my feelings: “It isn’t just symptomatic of a desperate race to secure the necessary utilities: it’s also one of the clearest signs yet that the AI industry has turned its back on the growing climate crisis in favor of pollution-spewing gas generators it’s installing across the globe.” Indeed. It’s one thing to be racing to be a leader in this field, but to turn to polluting, climate-destroying gas power plants instead of solar and wind power, that’s absolutely disappointing and — frankly — morally disgusting.

For the heck of it, to see what this company’s AI bot thought about the power choice it made, I decided to ask Claude “Are gas power plants harmful to our climate?” The response was as follows:

“Yes, though they’re less harmful than coal and more harmful than most alternatives.

“Bottom line: Gas is a cleaner fossil fuel, not a clean one. Its climate impact is best judged by what it replaces (coal vs. renewables) and by how tightly methane leaks are controlled. Carbon capture could reduce plant emissions, but it’s still costly and not widely deployed.”

So, yeah, when you’re choosing to buy $3.4 billion worth of gas power plants instead of renewable energy power plants, that is without a doubt going to be a horrible decision for our climate. I’m sure if I asked Claude about the risk humans race from climate change, the answer would not be uplifting. But I’m not going to go there. Instead, I’ll turn back to Futurism for this summary: “Researchers have found that the effects of AI on the environment are nothing short of devastating. And the prognosis for the future is grim. Last month, environmental nonprofit Sierra Club estimated that upcoming AI data centers could release 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, wiping out nearly 15 years worth of greenhouse gas reduction efforts.”

Indeed — we’re facing drastic increases in emissions from the very dirty AI industry. The good news is people are already showing they’re fed up with AI data centers. Apparently, out of 41 ballot measures related to data centers that were up for a vote in the recent midterm elections, only one (1) went the way of the AI industry. That said, I don’t see investments in growth stopping right now, as is evidenced by this $3.4 billion gas engine order and OpenAI and others burning through billions of dollars a quarter.

#5621. What A Road Sign With A Black 'Y' Means (And Other Letters, Too)

We have covered all manner of weird road signs on Jalopnik before, including some seriously goofy ones. While oddities from around the globe are fun to explore and explain, it is a little more relevant to touch on road signs that crop up on U.S. soil. Some of these will no doubt be familiar, but others may not, so there is good reason to delve into them and provide a quick explainer. The black "Y" sign was the one that initially piqued our interest, which, by the way, highlights that a Y-shaped intersection is to be found up ahead. That led us to look at other weird letter- and symbol-focused road signs drivers may come across.

The obvious candidates are "P" for parking areas and "H" that marks hospitals, which are universally understood, but throughout this article, we will also explore what those weird "T" or upturned "U" signs mean, in addition to winding "S" and plus-symbol signs. That includes where drivers are most likely to find them and how best to react when they do. Listed in no particular order, here are our picks of eight letter- or symbol-focused road signs that we thought are worth exploring in a bit more detail.

As already explained briefly above, a sign that depicts a capitalized "Y" is there to let drivers know of a Y-shaped three-way intersection or a forked road ahead. The sign will typically be a diamond shape with a yellow background, which means it's a simple warning sign alerting drivers that the road splits. The choices of where to go are obvious — either left or right — but what might be less obvious is how the right of way is determined in a three-way intersection that isn't controlled by any other signs.

The general rule is that drivers must yield to the car on the right. Then there's always the first-to-arrive rule, which works as you would intend — the first to arrive at the split goes first. Of course, some drivers will assume right of way when it is not deserved, or perhaps they just do not see the other car(s). In such instances, it's best to yield to the other vehicle even if you believe you should have the right of way to ensure everyone gets past the intersection without incident.

When a road splits like this, it pays to be especially cautious. Drivers may attempt to dart from one lane to the next when correcting a last-minute wrong decision, plus motorbikes or cyclists could be hiding in your blind spots, so try to ensure you have sufficient space around you if possible. The NHTSA highlights that roughly one third of all traffic fatalities occur at signposted intersections, so doubling down on cautiousness here is never a bad idea, no matter how simple it may first appear.

Surprise surprise, the letter "T" on a road sign warns of a T-shaped intersection — we would hope that you managed to work that one out. The road you are traveling on is about to end and merge with another. Once again, this is a classic warning sign finished in a yellow and black colorway, on a diamond-shaped sign that lets drivers know something's coming up and they will have to act accordingly.

In this instance, drivers must yield to traffic on the intersecting road — they don't have the right of way here — before heading either left or right. There will usually be a stop or yield sign prior to the intersection itself, and to avoid any frustrating bumps with other drivers making late decisions, it's best to get into the required lane early rather than last-minute. Thankfully, of the deadliest intersections on U.S. roads, not many are T-shaped, but the same rules as above apply here. Give yourself space, keep an eye on your blind spots, and don't rush. Oh, and don't forget to use your turn signals either, even if you are in a dedicated turn lane.

Again, we won't be handing out prizes to anyone who is able to correctly guess this one. A cross or "plus" symbol indicates that a crossroad is coming up, and just like the other aforementioned sign, this too will be depicted on a black and yellow diamond-shaped warning sign. Here, traffic can and likely will be coming from all directions, so it's imperative to take the time that's needed and approach it with care. Be aware that drivers on the opposite leg might try to cross ahead of you as you pull out, and be sure to check traffic from both left and right directions. As always, make sure to follow the instructions depicted on any regulatory signs posted in your direction, as these might detail give-way instructions.

There is a good case to make here in favor of the roundabout. In many ways, it is a far better design than the traditional intersection, with fewer conflict points, no left-turns across the flow of traffic, and lower speeds. Roundabouts might seem perplexing to some, but according to data from the Federal Highway Administration, they have been proven to reduce injury and fatal crashes by 76% and 90%, respectively, plus they are far more time-efficient than traffic signals, so perhaps road users ought to just get used to them.

OK, that's not strictly true. This sign, which isn't an "S" at all — it's just a winding arrow — signifies that a winding road is up around. In other words, the natural habitat for a Miata owner who's looking for some engaging roads to make the most of their drop-top weekend car. Of course, the sign isn't actually there to tell drivers that the road is a great place to go hooning. Instead, it lets them know the road ahead has several curves one after another and that they should approach that section of road with some caution.

In fact, these "S" signs will frequently be accompanied by another advisory speed sign that suggests the maximum safe speed for the section. Drivers would be wise to pay attention to these speeds, as around 25% of all fatal road incidents happen on a curved section of road, with common causes being cars either drifting off into trees, rocks, or other fixed objects, or indeed drifting across the center of the road and causing a head-on collision with other traffic.

Anyone who can't figure this one out should probably start taking notes here. An upturned U-shaped arrow crossed out in red, of course, means that U-turns are not permitted. Drivers should continue on, take a left or right turn if available, and find another suitable route. Exceptions will not be made for those in classic red-and-white Gran Torinos.

This is the first sign featured on our list that strays from that typical yellow and black warning sign colorway. Instead, this is a rectangular regulatory sign with a white background. These signs can crop up just about anywhere, but they can commonly be spotted in business districts, on narrow streets, or busier stretches of the nation's roads, such as on multi-lane highways and freeways.

For those who may question the legality of U-turns when this sign isn't present, drivers can usually perform such a move in these circumstances: They should be in the leftmost or center-left lane, signalling their intention, and keeping an eye out for traffic as per any other manoeuvre.

A sideways "T" sign indicates that a side road is coming up. Depending on which way the T is oriented, the sign highlights whether the side road is on the right or the left. If the sign instead looks like an F or an E, but with an extended top or bottom, this means that two side roads are coming up on the right-hand side.

Specifically, this sign will appear when the side roads on the right are particularly close to one another. The hazard this poses to drivers on the major road is quite obvious; they should be wary of traffic entering from the right, and should be prepared to slow down. The sign itself is a typical diamond-shaped yellow-and-black warning sign, which does not indicate right of way. Typically, those on the major road will have the right of way, while those on the indicated side roads will have to yield to traffic on the major road.

The sign for a roundabout shows three arrows forming a circle, and once again, it will be a yellow-and-black diamond-shaped warning sign. Roundabouts always run in a counter-clockwise direction in North America. They can have numerous lanes and are an alternative to crossroads. Here, the right of way rules are simple and uniform: Drivers must always give way to traffic on the left — in other words, the cars that are already on the roundabout.

Getting the right lane is crucial for avoiding accidents; the leftmost lane is used for turning left, whereas the rightmost lanes are used for turning right, and both can be used for going straight on. These are the rules on multi-lane roundabouts unless signposted otherwise — this way, traffic in either lane does not cross unnecessarily.

As for whether drivers need to use turn signals on a roundabout or not, the answer is yes. It's never a bad idea to let other drivers know where you are going; even if you are comfortable in your own abilities to get across safely, it's best practice to help other motorists out by indicating to them your next intended move.

#5620. Injectable Nanobody Wins FDA Approval for Myasthenia Gravis

— Gefurulimab joins other approved C5 inhibitors

The FDA on Friday approved injectable gefurulimab (Klygefa), a dual-binding nanobody that blocks complement component 5 (C5) activation, to treat generalized myasthenia gravis in adults who are anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody positive.

The approval comes in the wake of the phase III PREVAIL trial, which randomized 260 adults with anti-AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis to receive weekly self-administered subcutaneous gefurulimab or placebo for 26 weeks. The trial met the primary endpoint, showing an improvement in scores on the Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) scale versus placebo at week 28, with a treatment difference of -1.6 points.

MG-ADL scores range 0-24 points; improvements emerged in week 1 and continued through week 26. Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis scores -- a key secondary endpoint -- also improved by week 4 compared with placebo, and improvement was sustained throughout the study.

The drug is available only through a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program. The drug carries a boxed warning for serious and life-threatening infections caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Three other C5 inhibitors have been approved by the FDA for myasthenia gravis: eculizumab (Soliris), ravulizumab (Ultomiris), and zilucoplan (Zilbrysq). All carry a similar warning, and patients are required to comply with recommendations for meningococcal vaccinations.

In PREVAIL, the percentage of participants with treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) was similar between the gefurulimab and placebo groups. Most TEAEs were mild to moderate (grade 1 or 2).

In the gefurulimab group, the most common TEAEs were injection site reactions (9.9%), headache (9.9%), and back pain (7.6%). Twelve people treated with gefurulimab had serious adverse events. One death occurred, which was not considered to be related to treatment.

Gefurulimab binds to serum albumin to provide an extended half-life, allowing once-weekly dosing. "The safety profile was in line with earlier studies of C5 inhibitors in generalized myasthenia gravis," observed Christiane Schneider-Gold, MD, and Ralf Gold, MD, both of Ruhr University Bochum in Germany, in a JAMA Neurology editorial earlier this year. "In addition, no unexpected safety concerns were identified in patients recruited across 20 countries," they wrote.

"Despite rather well-tolerated subcutaneous application, it remains an interesting matter which position gefurulimab will eventually gain in the continuously evolving treatment landscape in generalized myasthenia gravis and among the group of complement inhibitors," Schneider-Gold and Gold noted.

Data from the open-label extension of PREVAIL recently showed that gefurulimab sustained functional benefits through 52 weeks.

In September, the European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use recommended gefurulimab for EU approval.

#5619. What The US Midterm Elections Mean For Climate Progress

People across the United States voted in record numbers in last week’s incredibly consequential election, which has completely changed the makeup of Congress for its new term beginning in January 2027. The success of our electoral processes—still underway—should not be taken for granted. It’s a win for democracy when millions of citizens peacefully claim their right to a government of, by, and for the people.

Will the Trump administration acknowledge voters’ repudiation of its destructive agenda and work in cooperation with this new Congress? That remains to be seen, and I’m not holding my breath. But there’s no question that the shift in Congress has significant implications for the administration’s ability to continue to ram through its anti-science, authoritarian agenda—including on climate and clean energy issues.

Energy affordability concerns, opposition to proliferating data centers, and anger at corruption and extreme economic inequality were undoubtedly driving forces in how people voted. While not everyone explicitly named climate change as a top issue (although many did put it in their top three), its fingerprints are all over the issues a majority of voters did name in polls.

If you care about addressing the high costs of electricity and gas, then you must reckon with the fact that this current fossil energy crisis, unleashed by the Trump administration’s war against Iran, is an extreme manifestation of the risks of fossil fuel dependence. The benefits of a transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy—renewable energy that the Trump administration has relentlessly attacked, further driving up costs for consumers—are tremendous. If you are deeply concerned about the rapid, unregulated build-out of data centers, you know that it comes with huge risks for communities related to climate, water, pollution, health, and electricity cost burdens. And it’s so clear that the Trump administration’s corruption, lies about climate science, and massive giveaways to fossil fuel polluters are leaving us all bearing the high costs of climate damages while large corporations and the president’s inner circle are raking in enormous profits.

Here’s another reality: regardless of politics, climate change is here, and science shows it’s rapidly worsening with the world’s imminent overshoot of 1.5°C of global warming. Communities are already experiencing deadly and costly climate impacts, including extreme heatwaves, catastrophic wildfires, record-breaking flooding, drought, accelerating sea level rise, intense ocean heat, irreversible loss of glaciers and ice sheets, stresses to critical ecosystems and more. These impacts are showing up in people’s daily lives—harming their health, destroying homes, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure, raising insurance premiums, hammering businesses, stressing water supplies, and threatening food security and affordability.

Climate change and clean energy are pocketbook issues. They are a lot more than that, of course. And climate change does not care if you live in a red state or a blue state. (One can ask if that is that even a relevant frame after an election that scrambled all conventional wisdom about “red” and “blue” dichotomies.)

Importantly, we will soon have a Congress where a majority accepts the scientific evidence on climate change. (Yes, I also wish we could take that for granted in 2026, but not in US politics, sadly.) That’s an important start and means we can advocate for policymakers to legislate based on the facts, instead of being stuck fighting disinformation and lies.

Here’s what this seismic “change election” could mean for action on climate change, some cautions about what likely won’t change right away, and what we’ll have to keep fighting for.

We will have to keep fighting back in courts to hold the Trump administration accountable for egregiously flouting the law. We’ve already had a major win in a lawsuit where the administration was found to be violating the Federal Advisory Committee Act in secretly setting up a ‘Climate Working Group’ stacked with climate contrarians to draft a sham science report, which the EPA then used to justify its proposal to gut the Endangerment Finding. We’ve also filed suit against the administration for repealing the Endangerment Finding, contrary to law, science, and the public interest.

On the international front, the Trump administration has shamefully exited the bedrock UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and that won’t change as long as it is in power. As I write from COP31 in Türkiye, the administration’s abandonment of global climate cooperation is very much on my mind; it’s crucial for the rest of the world to forge ahead regardless of the high stakes. There is a real risk that a beleaguered Trump administration will double down on its authoritarian ways and continue to find new ways to disrupt global climate progress and multilateral institutions. But Congress now has the power and responsibility to keep this reckless administration in check and ensure it is held accountable, at home and on the global stage.

“Change elections” come weighted with the hopes and dreams of many. As climate justice advocates, we know that policymakers have pushed off meaningful climate action far too long, and those failures are putting us all at profound risk. Yet, deep-pocketed fossil fuel interests, Big Tech, and other powerful entities continue to obstruct and delay action, still hold all too much sway over both parties in Congress, and we can expect their harmful tactics to ratchet up. So now it’s our responsibility to fight for what comes next, to make our shared dreams come true. Because those dreams of a safer, more just world for generations of young people to come must become reality.

#5618. The Crucial Difference Between Flock Cameras And Plate Readers In Other Countries

Stories about Flock cameras and other stalkerish automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have been a mainstay of American news for the last year or two, and horror stories involving this questionable technology are everywhere. From police using ALPRs to stalk citizens to AI-powered ALPRs flagging innocent auto journalists for stealing vehicles, there's no shortage of evidence that ALPRs are making the world worse. A lot of such stories you see in the news and even here on Jalopnik are about misuse of and issues with ALPRs specifically in the United States, though. While there's certainly some bias toward American news on publications based in the States, it still does raise the question: Are there Flock cameras or equivalents in other countries? And if so, do they cause the same volume of issues?

The answer is an interesting one. First, yes, ALPRs do exist outside of the United States, though the technology is often called automatic number plate recognition, or ANPR, due to regional differences in how license plates are referred to. Nearly 100 countries use this technology to track automobile movement and other data. However, Flock cameras themselves aren't nearly as prevalent outside the United States. In fact, the big difference between the implementation of license plate recognition technology in the U.S. and abroad is in who owns it and how the data collected is managed.

See, Flock Safety and Axon, two of the biggest promulgators of ALPR tech in the States, are privately operated companies that contract their services out to the state via entities like police departments and city councils. In other countries, and European countries in particular, ALPRs are typically owned, deployed, and operated by the state itself, rather than subcontracted through private companies. This distinction might just make all the difference.

If you're skeptical that a state-owned surveillance network is different than a privately owned, state-sponsored surveillance, well, you know, that's fair. But there are indeed some notable differences between how this technology is treated in the U.S. and how it's used abroad.

The rest of the world is certainly no stranger to surveillance. For example, the UK has a massive network of CCTV cameras that leave urban areas like London heavily monitored at all times, and they're now employing AI to level up their surveillance efforts, too. AI-powered surveillance is also rapidly ramping up in China, Brazil, and Australia.

Whether these networks are installed and operated by governments or private entities, the fact is that there's room for abuse by those with access to the data. However, in some other locations, it's easier for governments to regulate and oversee how the data is used. For example, European ALPR data is protected by the region's General Data Protection Regulation, which is way more than we have here in the ALPR Wild West.

In the U.S., Flock data from one municipality can be accessed by basically anyone in other areas with a Flock contract, and hackers who pulled a Flock camera apart showed that it's pretty easy to get the stored data even without a contract. Some police officers have even been caught accessing Flock data after leaving the force, according to the Washington Post. When this happens, finding accountability can be hard. ALPRs owned and run by the state directly at least have clear channels for voicing dissent, though it may also be true that they're more entrenched and harder to remove.

#5617. 313 kW Rooftop Solar System at Virginia Elementary Will Save $581,000 in Energy Costs

Roanoke City Schools to Add 313 kW Solar Power System

Staunton, VA — Secure Solar Futures, a provider of on-site clean energy to schools, local governments, and businesses, will build a 313-kilowatt solar power system installed at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, VA. Construction of the system is expected later this year at no capital cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement with Secure Solar Futures. Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, a subsidiary of Pardee Resources Company, will provide the majority of the capital for the solar system.

A total of 531 bi-facial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, TX, will be installed on the rooftop of the school located at 3142 Preston Avenue, NW, and will offset 67% of the power used by the school annually.

In its first year, the school’s solar system will produce 421 megawatt hours of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes and provide environmental benefits by avoiding 371 metric tons of carbon pollution, which is equal to the emissions produced by 87 gasoline-powered passenger vehicles, or the carbon sequestered by 372 acres of U.S. forests, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Under the Power Purchase Agreement, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, together with its partner Secure Solar Futures, will own, operate, and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

During the term of the Power Purchase Agreement, Preston Park Elementary School will save $581,000 in net avoided costs for electricity. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s 35- to 40-year productive lifespan.

Roanoke City Public Schools (RCPS) is an urban school division in Roanoke, Virginia, serving a pre-K through 12th grade population of approximately 14,000 students. RCPS provides an inclusive and equitable, student-centered culture that empowers lifelong learning. Through meaningful, relevant, and engaging learning opportunities, we will empower all students to dream, excel, and meet their full potential to benefit our city and its citizens. The division has 17 elementary schools, five middle schools, two high schools, and five program locations, including the Roanoke Valley Governor’s School for Science & Technology and two career and technical education centers. Visit www.rcps.info for additional information.

#5615. More Measles Deaths Reported as U.S. Cases Top 5,400

— State health departments have now recorded 10 measles-related deaths

Wisconsin and Pennsylvania reported two more measles-associated deaths on Friday, as the U.S. stands on the brink of losing its measles elimination status with more than 5,400 cases.

Wisconsin health officials reported a measles-associated death in a child, without further detail. The state, which has now logged 649 cases since August, just last week reported its first such death since 1990. The death in Pennsylvania involved an unvaccinated resident, according to the state's health department, which didn't disclose further information.

Nationwide, 5,412 cases of measles have been confirmed as of Nov. 12, according to the CDC, the highest tally in decades. Nearly all -- 97% -- have been in unvaccinated people.

The CDC has confirmed six measles-related deaths this year, double the three it logged last year, but a number for 2026 that trails the 10 measles-related deaths reported by state health departments. With Friday's announcement, Pennsylvania has reported seven such deaths among its nation-leading 1,542 measles cases, Wisconsin two, while New York has recorded one death among its 210 cases.

The ongoing outbreaks will likely mean the end of the U.S. measles elimination status, first attained in 2000. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) met this week to determine whether the chain of measles transmission in the U.S. has gone on uninterrupted for at least a year, which would spell the end of the public health victory -- a decision by PAHO is expected imminently.

The outbreaks nationwide come as the vaccine skepticism of U.S. public health officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- a leading anti-vaccine activist before becoming the nation's top health official -- have sown doubt over the safety of the MMR shot and other vaccines.

The CDC cited safety concerns in its controversial move to recommend separate MMR and varicella vaccines, and the Trump administration has proposed separating the MMR vaccine's components into three individual shots, a recommendation that if implemented would almost certainly further decrease already-slipping U.S. vaccination rates.

The CDC earlier this year reported that 92.4% of 2025-26 kindergarteners got their required MMR shots. Prior to the COVID pandemic, that rate was at 95% -- the level needed for herd immunity.

#5614. Rocket Fuel: The Last Frontier For Natural Gas

Fossil fuels are slowly beginning to lose their grip on the global transportation sector, with one key omission: rocket fuel. The rocket fuel conundrum has earned an uptick in attention in recent years, now that rocket launches, once rare, are becoming as commonplace as rush hour traffic. The Elon Musk venture SpaceX, for example, is building new natural gas pipelines in order to produce its own methane-based propellant, needed to sustain the launch of many thousands of rockets in the coming years.

Not all rocket fuel is methane-based, but that’s where some aerospace firms, including SpaceX, have landed in the pursuit of space domination. Methane is processed from natural gas, stripping away nitrogen and other impurities. Liquefied and mixed with liquid oxygen, it becomes a powerful propellant.

With its future volume of launch operations in mind, SpaceX aims to exercise as much control as possible over its fuel supply. The company is investing in its own natural gas pipelines and on-site fuel production facilities to help ensure that the taps don’t run dry, though it still relies on the gas industry to find the stuff and bring it up from the ground.

SpaceX has already been sucking up a copious amount of natural gas for its existing operations in Texas and Florida. “SpaceX (SPCX) is emerging as one of the largest new customers for natural gas,” reported the oil and gas analytics firm East Daley in October.

“Unlike Falcon 9, which burns rocket-grade kerosene and liquid oxygen, Starship creates a direct link between launch activity and natural gas consumption. SPCX plans to process and liquefy pipeline gas into liquid methane to fuel the rockets,” East Daley elaborates.

As described by East Daley, the SpaceX subsidiary Coastal Connect Services is planning a 32.4-mile natural gas pipeline to hook up SpaceX operations in Cape Canaveral, Florida with existing infrastructure jointly owned by Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer.

Meanwhile, at the company’s launch site and newly incorporated (as of 2025) City of Starbase in Cameron County, Texas, plans are in motion for SpaceX affiliate Lone Star Mineral Development to connect the new 8-mile “Starpipe” natural gas pipeline with another 145-mile pipeline currently being built by the firms WhiteWater, Enbridge, and MPLX. Starpipe is expected to begin shuttling natural gas into Starbase Texas early next year.

The two pipeline projects come alongside word that SpaceX has nailed down approvals for parts of a new $100 billion project that expands the company’s US footprint into another combination city-and-launch-site under the name of Starbase, Louisiana. The new city will presumably also require a reliable supply of natural gas for on-site rocket fuel production.

For the record, Starbase, Louisiana is not part of the educational non-profit organization STARBASE Louisiana, an affiliate of the national STARBASE program of the US Department of Defense, aimed at stimulating interest in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) topics among 5th grade students. The Louisiana branch of STARBASE is located Barksdale Air Force Base in Bossier Parish, in the northwestern part of the state.

Starbase, Louisiana will take up 125,000 acres of land at Pecan Island in a marshy region along the southern coast in Vermilion Parish, where plans are being laid for 30 launches per day. More than a dozen launch towers will eventually sprout up at the site, where the operation will include producing rocket fuel.

If you’ve gotten wind of the project under the name “Osprey,” you’re not dreaming. The new city was reportedly code-named “Project Osprey” during initial discussions with public officials. As described by the Gulf State News affiliate WWNO (New Orleans Public Radio) on November 11, Project Osprey was shrouded in secrecy during the initial negotionas, with “dozens” of local officials signing non-disclosure agreements that limited what they could say about the project.

The Osprey code name also reportedly enabled Vermilion Parish officials to sidestep public participation in ostensibly public hearings on the Starbase, Louisiana project earlier this year. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry finally let the cat out of the bag in a public announcement in August. Local residents and the nonprofit organization Vermillion Citizens coalition have already filed a lawsuit against the project, alleging that parish officials approved parts of Starbase, Louisiana in violation of the state’s Open Public Meetings Law.

If and when shovels hit the ground on Starbase, Louisiana, the Trump administration is taking steps to help ensure that natural gas producers in the US come through with the goods — not just for SpaceX, of course, although the firm has become a market-mover in the gas industry as noted by East Daley.

On November 10, for example, the US Department of Energy announced the finishing touches on a $480 million loan in support of Project Elkhorn, an endeavor under the umbrella of the oil and gas firm Arena Energy. Project Elkhorn covers the modernization of 22 existing platforms off the Louisiana coast — coincidentally or not, the same state that expects to host the new Starbase city.

Arena launched in 1999 with a focus on revitalizing mature oil and gas fields. According to the Energy Department, Project Elkhorn will ramp natural gas production up to 77 million cubic feet per day at peak production among the 22 platforms, alongside up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day. By way of contrast, the 22 platforms currently produce 30,000 barrels of oil per day. Over the lifespan of Project Elkhorn, the collective total is expected to add 25 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas to the US fossil energy roster.

As CEO of the leading EV maker Tesla, Elon Musk has earned his share of credit for rescuing electric cars from the dustbin of automotive obscurity and vaulting them into the mainstream mobility market of today — if not so much here in the US, then certainly overseas. Musk’s other ventures, on the other hand, threaten to offset, if not override, whatever sustainability gains are to be made from EVs.

In addition to SpaceX, Musk’s xAI data centers have also contributed to spiking demand for natural gas. Last year word dropped that Musk’s Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee trucked in approximately three dozen industrial-sized gas generators to power the site, at least 15 of which were already in operation without an air quality permit. The Southern Environmental Law Center has been among those raising the alarm over toxic emissions from the generators, which lack the pollution controls required of permanent power plants.

Natural gas also factors into a new data center planned for the SpaceX-backed City of Starbase, Texas, which sits adjacent to Brownsville. The city of Brownsville recently imposed a temporary moratorium on new data center construction. According to ABC News affiliate KVUE and other sources, earlier this year Elon Musk asked Brownsville officials to de-annex a parcel of land at its outskirts, evidently in order to building a $24 billion data center at the site along with a new gas-fired power plant for a new data center to be located in Starbase. The request was granted, enabling the project to skirt around the Brownsville moratorium.

Starbase city officials are scheduled to conduct a public hearing on the new data center on December 9, where presumably they will decide whether or not the project can make due with gas generators until a full gas power plant with appropriate pollution controls can materialize.

Over and above the rocket fuel issue, grassroots activists, environmental organizations, and researchers have been raising the alarm over the impact of Starbase in Texas for years, tracking significant harm to local public recreation resources as well as wildlife habitats. Similar concerns have surfaced around SpaceX’s plans for Starbase, Louisiana.

Of course, nobody seriously expects the whole domestic rocket business to stop in its tracks. The issue is one of mitigating climate and biodiversity risks, developing projects that avoid pummeling vulnerable communities with additional public health risks, and investing in more sustainable options including alternative rocket fuels.

Keep an eye on the aviation industry for some hints at the future of sustainable propellants. Airline stakeholders have been focusing on SAF, generally meaning a bio-based equivalent of kerosene jet fuel. However, the going has been slow, and it’s even slower in the field of propellants. The European Space Agency, for example, has been exploring green propellants for space operations for 25 years, with little to show for its efforts.

More recently, though, aviation stakeholders have begun turning to the emerging electrofuels or “solar fuels” industry, meaning fuels synthesized from captured carbon and green hydrogen, with solar and other renewables powering the operation. The green hydrogen industry has been struggling for traction, but signs of scaleup have finally emerged, with e-kerosene jet fuel in play along with green hydrogen. Honda, for one, is envisioning a fleet of reusable rockets propelled by renewable fuels, and at least two Chinese firms are also working the reusable rocket angle.

#5613. This Honda Civic Is The Direct Ancestor Of The OG Tesla Roadster

Tom Gage is the one-time CEO of a company you probably don't remember, called AC Propulsion. However, that firm was one of the progenitors of EVs and, by extension, Tesla. Gage is also the one-time owner of this 1994 Honda Civic. This past weekend he sold it, and we should explain why that's important.

See, underneath its aged sheet metal, it wasn't a Civic at all, but more of a science experiment. It has no tailpipe because Gage's partner, AC Propulsion co-founder Alan Cocconi, gutted the little hatchback in 1994 to fill with lead-acid bricks and convert the Civic into a proof-of-concept electric car that led to the rise of Tesla. The Tesla link is that AC Propulsion used the Civic to try out systems that would later debut on the company's 1998 tzero electric Roadster. That car looked cooler, but had the same tech that powered the electric Honda. And it's that technology that Tesla eventually licensed in 2004 and that ended up featuring in the original Tesla Roadster in 2008.

We interviewed Gage, who explained that it wasn't electric propulsion (at first) that attracted Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard to EVs — and, eventually, Elon Musk. It was actually its sexy shape, which was just a kit car called the Piontek Sportech. "I mean, that was exactly the reason we built the tzero in the first place," Gage explains. "EVs still had this golf cart image, and so even with lead-acid batteries, the tzero would be zero to 60 in the four-second range." This is funny because, actually, the Honda was just as fast. The tale of how AC Propulsion went from gutting Civics to making electric Scions and, eventually, helping spawn the iconic Tesla Roadster, is fascinating. It even includes a bit of spying, too.

Some of Cocconi's engineering that made it into this 1994 Honda Civic was way ahead of its time. For instance, Gage says Cocconi devised a module that could produce AC-to-DC (and vice-versa) power flow. "When you were driving, [it] could take the DC current from the battery and convert it to high-frequency AC to run the motor. And when you weren't driving, and you plugged it in, the same inverter components would convert the AC from the grid into DC to charge the battery."

Modern EVs have this capability, but even today, something Cocconi worked on isn't ubiquitous — feeding power from the EV back to your home or to the grid. AC Propulsion cars were eventually capable of that at up to 20 kilowatts, while the 2027 Ford Fathom will be able to do this without a wall inverter at 10 kW.

According to Gage, the Civic had the first iteration of the 200-horsepower system, which the firm called a power electronics unit because it was more than just the motor and inverter. It contained that, as well as the charger, and the ability to push out a 12-volt DC power supply, which the Civic (or any car) needs since all of its components run on 12 volts.

Even back in the 1990s, AC Propulsion was looking for solutions that still bedevil carmakers today. For instance, how do you get reasonable all-electric range and fight battery weight simultaneously? At first, because the company was working with lead-acid batteries, they were stuck with limited range, and those batteries were far heavier than later lithium cells. Gage says that with batteries aboard, the Civic exceeded the gross vehicle limit of what the chassis was designed for, with the batteries alone weighing 1,200 pounds.

Fixing this required fitting a trailer with a gas engine aboard to operate as a range-extending generator, which topped up the batteries while driving. This created a series hybrid rather than a parallel hybrid, and the difference is that series hybrids only run their gas motors as generators — the engines don't power the wheels. Hence, putting the motor on a trailer works just fine. "We had several generations," Gage laughed. "We had some kind of a Generac standard generator, which we modified in various ways, but the exhaust was really stinky and [it] didn't have that much power."

They eventually turned to Kawasaki, using the engine from the Ninja 250, which cranked at 11,000 rpm. "It was a little noisy," Gage quips. But it enabled the little Honda to get a remarkable 81 mpg. Later, AC Propulsion would adopt lithium-ion laptop batteries, and finally they could ditch needing to tow a gasoline engine to power an electric motor.

AC Propulsion went from their lead-acid-battery Civic in 1994 to the tzero in 1998. It initially also ran on lead-acid batteries. That problem was eventually solved in 2003, when AC Propulsion adopted lithium-ion batteries for the tzero. And this was huge for performance and range. "That was what drew the attention of the founders of Tesla," Gage says, referring to Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard. "Just getting the lithium-ion batteries, the tzero went from 80 to a 100-mile range to a 300-mile range with a 600-pound weight reduction."

Eberhard became an early investor in AC Propulsion and wanted to purchase one of the tzeros. But mass production, according to Gage, was out of the question, since the cars would have to sell for $220,000, and AC Propulsion told Eberhard they were losing $100,000 on every tzero they made. But Eberhard still had sports car dreams, which turned out to be fortunate for him. Around this time, Gage and Cocconi were trying to attract another investor, a man named Elon Musk. They didn't want Musk's money to make more tzeros, but to transform the future of transportation.

"What the world really needs is a low-cost, high-utility vehicle," Gage says. But Musk, like Eberhard, didn't care about cars for the masses. "It was too mundane for him," Gage recalls. "He wanted to do something like the tzero. So I introduced him to Martin [Eberhard]." That's how Tesla got started. From 2004, rather than outright build Teslas, AC Propulsion would license its tzero technology to the startup. This would later help spawn the 2008 Tesla Roadster — the predecessor to the new Roadster that's boring and doesn't really fly, according to your takes.

Gage and Cocconi's next big idea wouldn't turn out to be anything as consequential as they'd hoped. They were converting Scion xBs into EVs, and AC Propulsion called that car the eBox. Gage explains they chose the Scion because it was practical and cheap. "It's got some of the best rear seat ingress and egress of any car ever built, in my opinion. Maybe that's a small thing, but you know, it was just a super utilitarian design." As Gage also explains, that Scion seemed "iconoclastic." And there was the matter of a tall-riding box, the better for stuffing batteries aboard. Unfortunately, the second-generation xB was a lot heavier than the first. "We realized the importance of lightweight to make the end product as good as it could be," he says, so they explored working with Nissan instead.

Nissan did oblige — but with an ulterior motive, according to Gage. "They ended up sending a bunch of engineers over several times to drive the eBox and look at it. We thought we were trying to work a deal with them where they would provide us with rolling chassis or some kind of supply arrangement." But that's not what Gage suspects was actually happening. "Turns out, what they were really doing was scoping out what we were doing," because Nissan was researching its own EV. "Then a year or two later, they came out with the Leaf." The Leaf is still on the market, and Nissan recently came out with a Leaf Nismo.

There's a kicker to this story. Gage worked in the battery division of AC Propulsion until 2011, and he noticed that the Civic was just gathering dust. So he bought it for $100. "I forget when they stopped driving it, but it was just parked in the back lot. I offered them 100 bucks for it, and they sold it." Not that it was a gem, or even running, Gage explains. "One of the employees at one point asked if he could turn it into a race car, and he started to tear it apart, but that's about as far as he got."

Gage says that this employee's ambitious plan included rewiring it and making a different adapter for the battery pack to switch from lead-acid to lithium-ion batteries. "I just know they wanted to get rid of it, and so I took it on, and I've been storing it ever since here," meaning at his house in Southern California. He thought about switching over from lead-acid to lithium-ion, which he figured would yield a car with up to 600 miles of range. He also thought of just going for broke with, "Super high-power lithium batteries, and then have a bit of a rocket ship, you know, because it would be much lighter than the average EV would and still have 200 horsepower."

Whether that's the Civic's destiny is unclear. But the good news is that the buyer already owns an AC Propulsion car, a Honda CRX the company converted in the early '90s. Gage called him a "worthy buyer." To this, we can only add that we hope there's another chapter to this story when the Civic is once again burning rubber under electric power.

#5610. Hummer H1s May Be Nearly Indestructible, But Some Serious Flaws Live In That 'Nearly' Part

The Hummer brand officially launched in 1992 with the debut of its AM General High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle military-based civilian model. Much like the popularity of the Willys Jeep in post-WWII America, the H1 capitalized on rah-rah post-Gulf War nationalism and a personal endorsement from Arnold Schwarzenegger to find its place in the automotive zeitgeist. After being awarded its first military production contract in 1983, the big diesel-powered machine was well-proven by the time John Q. Public could place an order a decade later. If the HMMWV can be relied on by our fighting finest in the Muthanna Province, then surely it'll withstand the rigors of your suburban commute, right? Well, as it turns out, the answer is a cryptically Schrödinger-esque yes and no.

When it comes to imposing four-wheeled machines, there's nothing quite as eye-catching and road-commanding as the original Hummer. Between 1992 and 1999, the vehicle was sold in small quantities by AM General's civilian division, but General Motors purchased the rights to market and distribute the Hummer brand for the new millennium. With just shy of 12,000 units sold across the truck's entire production run, these things are a bit thin on the ground, but they maintain a strong cultural significance today, and the appeal of a genuine mil-spec vehicle is hard to deny.

Because of its high profile and rarity, every variant of the H1 generally still commands a pretty penny, even two decades after production ended. A high-mileage early non-turbo diesel model might bring as low as $35,000, while a low-mileage 2006-only H1 Alpha runs into the low six-figure range. If you're going to be spending that much money to get yourself one of these rolling monuments of gender-affirming care, what trouble should you expect and look out for? Let's dig into it.

The first issue is that, simply due to their size and material density, they're really heavy. At around 7,500 pounds, you're moving a lot of metal around. Weight translates to atrocious fuel economy, like about 10 miles per gallon bad. Another downside: due to the military-based nature of these trucks, driver comfort is hardly a concern, and the noise, vibration, and harshness engineers were not really consulted in the design phase. According to a Hagerty review, the "engine sounds like a jackhammer inside the cockpit." Oh, and it doesn't have airbags.

On the plus side, a Hummer H1 is mostly indestructible, except for one major flaw. If you're a long-time reader of Jalopnik, you'll probably know where this is going, because over a decade ago our own Doug Demuro found out firsthand what breaks on the Hummer H1. I'll let him explain it.

"Beginning in about 1996, every single Hummer was fitted with a 6.5-liter Detroit Diesel turbodiesel V8, which combined the 194 horsepower of a Toyota Camry with the 438 lb-ft of torque from an angry farm tractor.

Well, there was one little issue: every single one of these engines was manufactured with a casting flaw that resulted in a crack on the number eight cylinder. Fortunately, the fix was easy: you just replaced the engine.

But check this out: it affected every single Hummer manufactured from 1996 to 2000... Every single Hummer built from 1996 to 2000 has either had its engine fail due to the number eight cylinder issue, or will have its engine fail."

The pre-1996 non-turbo Detroit Diesel-powered models, the rare gasoline-powered model, and the 2001-2006 models are unaffected. Check the engine casting number and make sure it was made after March 15, 1999.

There is another major issue with Hummer H1 trucks, but it's significantly less catastrophic than a failed engine. The onboard tire inflation-deflation system leaks because, of course, it does. Especially after a couple of decades of sitting on display with low-mileage odometers, the rubber lines of the system tend to crack and drop pressure. It's possible to replace all of the lines and make it function again, and there are ways to bypass the system altogether and inflate your tires the old-fashioned way.

There are plenty of other issues that come with buying a twenty-year-old truck. Just like anything with decades of wear, keep an eye on worn suspension components, leaks, rust, ill-maintained brakes, and maintenance records. According to TireRack.com, a set of H1 tires will cost up to $2,240, so that information might help you negotiate. Also, because this is a rare machine, you probably won't find any of the parts you need for things like the tire inflation system at your local corner parts store. The parts exist, but you might want to keep the Hummer Parts Guy on speed dial.

There are plenty of options for '96 to 2000 trucks that haven't had their engines replaced yet. If you can get one for cheap, it might make the basis of an interesting project truck. I'm imagining a rare two-door pickup H1s with a Duramax "Mongoose" 8.3-liter turbo diesel V8, the one found in the current Chevrolet and GMC HD trucks making 555 horsepower and 1,230 lb-ft of torque. That might be the only way to make an actually fast Hummer.

#5609. Sonnen, SOLRITE, & ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets

SOLRITE Unveils Next-Gen Virtual Power Plant Node with sonnen and ADAPT Energy, Integrating VPP Breakers to Turn Home Loads into Flexible Grid Assets

ADAPT Energy’s control of VPP breakers will add dispatchable load flexibility to the SOLRITE sonnen VPP, while paving a simpler, faster, and lower-cost path to whole-home backup

SOLRITE, a company specializing in developing, financing, and owning Virtual Power Plant Agreement (VPA) projects, together with Sonnen, a leader in Virtual Power Plant energy storage technology, announced they will now digitally integrate VPP smart breakers, managed by ADAPT Energy, into the SOLRITE  sonnen VPP. The integration marks the next evolution of sonnen and SOLRITE’s industry-leading partnership in VPP innovation, expanding beyond battery storage by transforming residential electrical loads into flexible, dispatchable grid assets for both the VPP and smart backup power applications.

Unlike traditional approaches to whole-home backup, often requiring hard-wired circuit relocation, including exclusive loads panels, the newly expanded VPP Node combines the sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to intelligently manage major household loads. This creates a more streamlined approach to whole-home backup while unlocking an entirely new source of flexibility for the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. With homeowner permission, the VPP smart breaker—controlled by ADAPT Energy—can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be flexible for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and Founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The integration addresses one of the longstanding challenges of whole-home backup: how to provide broad electrical coverage without having large household loads drain available battery capacity too quickly or cause the nano-grid to immediately fail after an off-grid transition due to excessive inrush current. With the newly expanded VPP smart breaker technology digitally integrated with the sonnen ecosystem, the system can intelligently shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns. This significantly reduces installation complexity and tedious inspections for installers, allowing crews to complete more jobs per week.

For homeowners, the system provides the convenience of a whole-home electrical configuration that intelligently manages the loads that have the greatest impact on backup duration. This work is all done in the background, meaning homeowners do not have to worry about resetting individual circuits during an outage. Instead, participating homes will see more value from their VPA program in the form of an enhanced backup power experience. Furthermore, at any time in the future, if a homeowner is interested in altering which of their VPP smart breaker-controlled loads are shed during an outage, the process to make such a change is quick and easy, requiring no electrical reconfiguration.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, President of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

The permission-based architecture aligns the interests of the homeowner, battery owner and utility. The real opportunity comes when homeowners choose to opt in to allow the breakers to participate in on-grid VPP events.

When a VPP event is dispatched, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge in concert with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads, and by using Eaton AbleEdge breakers, ADAPT achieves this right where the breaker sits, without relocation. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid. That way, the VPP can respond through both energy stored in the battery and energy that would have otherwise been consumed by the home, thereby increasing the dispatched injection into the grid, by the VPP.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, Chairman and CEO of sonnen Inc. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”

#5608. Are AI Data Centers a Health Concern?

— Regulations should focus on safety and equity as centers scale up

With the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) has been thrust into the mainstream -- incorporated into various industries as well as our personal lives. In healthcare, AI scribes are prominent, and peers use OpenEvidence as part of their clinical practice. While AI has its benefits, we cannot deny the immense health and environmental costs, which are only growing as more hyper-scale data centers (which can span more than 17 football fields) are rapidly developed.

Communities nationwide are fighting this. With moratoriums and calls for scaling back on development, we must take advantage of this opportunity to ensure the creation of safe policies and regulations. Data centers should be the size necessary to run basic functions but no larger; they must be sustainably built, and include transparency and community input throughout all stages of development; and they cannot perpetuate the harms and injustices that many communities have historically faced.

Data centers require large amounts of energy to run AI processes. Unfortunately, in part because of their rapid development and need for energy, we have postponed closing fossil fuel generators that were slated to shutter in 2025.

When fossil fuels are burned, they emit pollutants that are linked to poor health outcomes such as premature death, lung diseases, cognitive decline, and heart attacks. An analysis of a Virginia data center found its air emissions could cost between $53 million and $99 million annually in health-related impacts. Another study found that AI's contribution to air pollution could result in 1,300 premature asthma-related deaths in 2030.

Meanwhile, short-term exposure to PM2.5 was attributed to 1 million premature deaths from 2000-2019, which is concerning given that these data centers are continuously spewing air pollutants. Furthermore, fence-line communities -- predominantly Black, Latino, and low-income communities -- already face disproportionate health impacts due to living near polluting infrastructures, and in some places are disproportionately sited to have more data centers developed near them compared to other communities.

Data centers use copious amounts of potable water, not just to cool their servers, but also to generate the electricity that powers the centers. Many data centers are built in drought-prone areas, stressing communities already facing water scarcity, and increasing the risk of dehydration, waterborne illnesses such as dengue, and related mental health consequences.

Electricity generation drives much of data centers' water usage. Between Texas, California, Georgia, Ohio, Illinois, Arizona, and Virginia, 3.4 trillion gallons of freshwater were used annually for data center electricity, which is about 12 times the water used to power data centers in Los Angeles, Washington, DC, and Phoenix combined.

Communities are also concerned about water pollution. For example, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS or "forever chemicals") may leak and be released into soil and groundwater systems. PFAS are difficult to remove and have been linked to birth defects, cancer, and heart and brain diseases. Additionally, water used as a coolant can be released back into water supplies hotter than it was before, disrupting aquatic ecosystems and biological processes important to the functioning of our planet.

Diesel generators, cooling towers, and the machinery in data centers emit persistent noises that have caused distress to communities. The World Health Organization states that noise pollution is linked to increased mental health issues like heart attacks, strokes, or poor academic performance in children, and infrasound (waves that can be felt but not heard, and aren't easily blocked by windows or buildings) are linked to anxiety, headaches, stress, vertigo, and insomnia.

Some parts of data centers, like cooling towers, can reach up to 70 decibels within 400 feet, and industrial-sized diesel generators can reach 105 decibels. Data centers continuously emit these noises and sound waves. And we anticipate that vulnerable neighborhoods already facing noise exposure inequities from transportation or aviation will continue to bear this burden with further development of data centers.

Though not as discussed as much, data centers should also take caution with how they are built, lest they contribute to light pollution, which impacts our circadian rhythm, which disrupts sleep, and is linked to impaired attention and memory, dementia, obesity, hypertension, and mood disorders like depression.

Health professionals can play an important role in responsible AI usage and expansion to prevent the perpetuation of injustices that put communities at further environmental and health risks. There are actions we can take now:

While not an exhaustive list, we can take personal and community actions to advocate for responsible AI and data center development and fulfill the promise we made to do no harm.

The views of the author do not necessarily reflect those of the Medical Society Consortium on Climate and Health or its members.

Carelon was hit with a lawsuit in April over the alleged ghost networks and their impact on the Empire Plan in particular. In the case, plaintiff's attorneys conducted secret shopper calls to analyze Carelon's network, calling 300 providers. Just 17% of those contacted took insurance and were open to new patients.
