#5590. Bon Secours Mercy Health bumps up offer for majority stake in Surgery Partners to $6B valuation

Bon Secours Mercy Health bumps up offer for majority stake in Surgery Partners to $6B valuation" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Bon Secours Mercy Health bumped the price tag on its pending transaction to acquire a majority share in healthcare services company Surgery Partners in response to an unsolicited offer the short-stay surgical platform received from a third party, the organizations shared this week.

The transaction now values the acquiree at $6 billion, or $25 per share, up from the initial $5.7 billion and $23.50 per share (see that story below). Additionally, the parties agreed to an additional $1.61 per share in ticking fees if the deal doesn't close by March 1, 2027.

The companies' announcement does not name the third party, which offered $28 per share in a Nov. 3 proposal. A report from Bloomberg, citing an unnamed source, names UnitedHealth as the extra bidder whose offer was rejected over concerns about deal complexity and ability to close.

Surgery Partners’ business platform includes ambulatory surgery centers, surgical hospitals and about 5,000 affiliated physicians spanning 30 states. It reported $3.31 billion in revenue during 2025 and $0.47 adjusted earnings per share.

Affiliates of Bain Capital Private Equity currently control about 39% of Surgery Partners. Under the current deal, Bain would roll over its shares while the remainder would be acquired by a Bon Secours affiliate, HealthSpan Partners.

Bon Secours Mercy Health is acquiring a majority share in healthcare services company Surgery Partners in a take-private deal valuing the acquiree at $5.7 billion, the organizations announced Monday morning.

The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of next year, pending approvals, and with over 200 locations in tow, would help the major nonprofit health system create “one of the country’s largest outpatient surgical care platforms,” they said.

“As healthcare continues to evolve, it is important to grow in ways that allow us to serve more people, in more communities and through a broader range of care settings,” John M. Starcher, Jr., president and CEO of Bon Secours Mercy Health, said in the announcement. “Our relationship with Surgery Partners represents an important step toward advancing that commitment."

Currently, affiliates of Bain Capital Private Equity control about 39% of the public Surgery Partners. Under the terms of the deal, Bain Capital would retain and roll over those shares, while HealthSpan Partners, an affiliate of Bon Secours, would purchase the remainder with cash at $23.50 per share.

Surgery Partners’ short-stay surgical platform includes ambulatory surgery centers, surgical hospitals and about 5,000 affiliated physicians spanning 30 states. It reported $3.31 billion in revenue during 2025 and $0.47 adjusted earnings per share.

The company has been public since 2015, with a 2017 merger making it the largest standalone, independent surgical facilities operator at the time. Bain Capital made an offer in January 2025 to fully acquire the shares it didn’t own for $25.75 apiece (roughly $6.7 billion enterprise valuation), though that offer was rejected a few months later.

Surgery Partners has also been slimming down some of its acute care holdings in recent months, a strategic move its leadership said would better position the company as a purely short-stay surgical provider while limiting its exposure to Medicaid.

“We believe this transaction represents the best path forward for Surgery Partners, delivering an attractive all-cash premium to our shareholders while creating lasting benefits for our patients, physicians and other stakeholders,” Surgery Partners CEO Eric Evans said Monday.

Bon Secours Mercy Health is a Catholic nonprofit with 47 hospitals, more than 1,200 care sites and nearly 60,000 employees. It reported just shy of $14 billion in total operating revenue through 2025, as well as $324 million of recurring operating income (2.3% recurring operating margin) and a $1.1 billion bottom line. Of note, its holdings include 41% ownership in revenue cycle management company Ensemble Health Partners, for which a summer strategic recapitalization transaction with a new private equity investor injected $670.8 million in cash into the system, per recent financial statements.

Bon Secours’ HealthSpan Partners is financing the Surgery Partners purchase with a combination of cash on hand and newly secured debt. Upon closing, the parties plan to keep Surgery Partners’ operations, brand and headquarters in place, while also keeping the business as a secular organization.

Strategically, the deal is evidence of large health systems’ growing investments in ambulatory care networks, where many expect to see rising demand as consumers prioritize lower-cost care settings. Healthcare executives have bluntly described these investments as a “top priority,” particularly as regulatory and policy activity such as the wind-down of Medicare’s inpatient-only list pushes care outside of the hospital.

“As more care moves beyond the hospital setting, patients are looking for high-quality care that fits more seamlessly into their lives,” Wael Haidar, M.D., Bon Secours Mercy Health’s president of clinical operations, said in the announcement. “Surgery Partners understands that care should be designed around the needs of patients, and that approach aligns closely with our mission. Together, we have an opportunity to expand access to high-quality outpatient care while supporting physicians and helping patients receive the right care, in the right setting, at the right time.”

The most apparent analogue for Bon Secours’ deal comes from Ascension, an even larger Catholic nonprofit, which closed a $3.9 billion deal over the summer to acquire AMSURG, an ambulatory surgery management services company with over 300 locations. Ascension CEO Eduardo Conrado has described that deal as both a means to flesh out his system’s existing markets—improving overall volumes and allowing hospitals to focus on high-complexity patients—and a way to strike new business partnerships with other local health systems in markets beyond its prior footprint.

#5589. Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch

Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.

Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.

Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication

One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.

This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.

However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.

Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.

A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.

For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.

Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered

To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:

The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.

Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.

The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later

Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.

Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.

However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.

These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.

Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.

Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?

Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.

Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.

Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.

Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.

Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.

Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.

The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy

Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.

Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.

Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.

But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.

Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.

Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?

Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.

Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.

If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.

However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.

For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

#5588. No Surprises Act IDR claims cost employer plans an additional $8.4B last year, study finds

No Surprises Act IDR claims cost employer plans an additional $8.4B last year, study finds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The No Surprises Act's independent dispute resolution process cost employer plans $8.39 billion in 2025, according to a new analysis.

Researchers at the Employee Benefit Research Institute combed federal IDR data and found that these additional costs equal about 63 cents per $100 spent by employer-based insurance plans. The total includes $4.73 billion in costs incurred in the first half of the year as well as $3.66 billion in the second half of 2025.

Even when EBRI analysts used different thresholds to exclude outlier awards, such as costs that were unusually high, they still landed on an estimate of at least $8.02 billion, per the study.

The researchers note that this data doesn't necessarily paint the full picture, as it only encompasses cases that proceeded to IDR. The study doesn't include information on claims that were settled outside of arbitration, administrative costs, any changes in networks or provider rates or the cost associated with patient protections.

The study calculates additional cost by taking the IDR award amounts and subtracting the plan's initial payment and any cost-sharing from the patient.

"These new data provide a clearer picture of what health plans owe for out-of-network services beyond their initial payments, after accounting for patient cost sharing,” said Paul Fronstin, Ph.D., director of Health Benefits Research at EBRI, in the announcement. “Separating those amounts from arbitration awards allows us to measure additional plan obligations more directly."

The study also doesn't project the impact of IDR on premiums, and the researchers said that having greater insight into the administrative expenses and other ancillary costs would be necessary to understand how the No Surprises Act's processes may impact patients' costs directly.

The IDR processes have gained increasing scrutiny from health plans and plan sponsors as the number of disputes, and their associated payouts, rise. When a claim reaches the arbitration phase, the results overwhelming favor providers, as they won in 85% of disputes last year.

An analysis from Georgetown University, released in August, estimated that total costs associated with IDR reached $22 billion in 2025. There were 2.6 million disputes initiated in 2025; by comparison, federal estimates projected about 22,000 cases annually reaching the arbitration phase.

Providers have pushed back on criticism of IDR, arguing that the root cause is payers undercutting them during the opening negotiation phase by setting low qualifying payment amounts for claims.

#5587. Historic New England City Reclaims Top Spot as America’s Hottest Market

A Connecticut metro known for its insurance headquarters and the Pratt & Whitney aerospace company has reclaimed its title as America's hottest housing market.

The Hartford, CT, metro area has shot back to the No. 1 spot in October for the first time since a summer run at the top from May through July 2026, according to the Realtor.com® October Hottest Markets report. Hartford has ranked in the top 20 a total of 57 times, claiming the crown eight times.

The Nutmeg State accounts for four of the top 20 markets, with Waterbury, New Haven, and Norwich joining Hartford with median list prices between $400,000 and $460,000, says the report.

The No. 1 market encompasses the cities of Hartford, West Hartford, and East Hartford, but also a large swath of quintessential historical towns that look like they stepped out of a Hallmark movie.

Those small towns—including Wethersfield, Windsor Locks, Avon, and Farmington—draw homebuyers with their small-town charm, stunning nature, and commutable locations.

They also offer relative affordability compared to the elite suburbs dotting the Long Island Sound, such as Greenwich, Westport, and Darien, which are closer to New York City.

But Hartford, the state's capital, is still close enough that it embraces some spillover from the more expensive areas. If residents need to commute to New York City only a couple of times a week, the approximately 2.5-hour drive or Amtrak ride may be worth it for the nature, safety, quiet, and relative affordability these small towns offer.

"Located in New England, midway between Boston and New York, Hartford is an ideal landing spot for homebuyers looking to take advantage of the relatively low home prices in an otherwise pricey part of the country," says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

And home browsers are most definitely interested.

The Hartford metro had 4.1 times the viewers per property as the rest of the country, by far the highest. Median days on the market are a swift 37 (only one more than last year and a month faster than the national time) and the median list price is $440,000, the second-highest among the top 10, behind only Manchester-Nashua, NH, at $549,000.

Homes in the most wanted markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on the market of 37 days, more than three weeks faster.

The hottest markets for October 2026 are Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (4.1 times the national average); Kenosha, WI (2.8); Lancaster, PA (2.4); Rochester, NY (2.5); Manchester-Nashua, NH (2.8); Peoria, IL (2.4); Erie, PA (2.8); Rockford, IL (2.6); and Waterbury-Shelton, CT (2.8).

Incorporated in 1693, Glastonbury (named after the town in England) boasts the country's oldest continuously running ferry, to Rocky Hill across the Connecticut River. It also has the second-highest concentration of surviving pre-1800s Colonial homes, about 154.

An easy 15-minute commute to Hartford via Route 2, and abutting both West Hartford and East Hartford, Glastonbury has long been a home base for the higher-ups in both the nearby insurance industry and Pratt & Whitney ("Pratt rats," in local lingo).

The past few decades have seen major changes for the formerly rural town as sprawling, multimillion-dollar estates began flecking the hills that were only farmland and tobacco fields not long ago.

Glastonbury has managed to retain much of its historical and rural appeal even as the town gained both a Whole Foods and a Trader Joe's, and its median home price skyrocketed, currently standing at $530,300, a 6.2% increase over last year.

Wendy Anderson of William Pitt Sotheby's International Realty, who represents the town's most expensive listing, a $7.2 million French chateau-style estate in South Glastonbury, says the town continues to draw high earners not only from Hartford, but from New York City and New Haven as well.

"It's always been a strong market, a sought-after town," she tells Realtor.com. "It's an easy commute."

Beyond the commute, the town—which is fairly large for a "small town" at about 52 square miles, with three ZIP codes—seems to have it all.

Beyond its bustling commercial center—complete with shops, restaurants, coffee spots, and an urgent care clinic—the area still boasts working farms, orchards, two active wineries, a sandy-shored pond, and a riverfront park.

All public schools have a rating of 8 or higher out of 10 by Great Schools, drawing families.

The housing stock is diverse: In addition to the aforementioned Colonial homes, there are small ranches, grand estates, classic midcentury homes, newer townhomes, and upscale rentals. There are even senior and lower-income communities.

"A lot of towns in Hartford County have a lot of amenities and activities," says Anderson, who has lived in Glastonbury for 45 years. "And a great sense of community. There's town football, soccer, tennis. So many activities for children, and concerts. And it's easy to get to the shoreline, or to get to Boston or New York."

Anderson doesn't think the market will go up indefinitely.

"I think the market has peaked, the wave has crested," she says. "But the market is still holding strong."

Since listing the $7.2 million French chateau on nearly 2 acres in July, she has already shown the estate to a dozen potential buyers—and just closed on a $1.4 million home that was sold in less than a week.

Buyers, usually business owners, are lured to the town by its spectacular fall colors, its rolling hills and dense forests, its fruit orchards, its gourmet restaurants and cosy taverns—as well as its relative affordability.

Adds the agent: "I just saw a TikTok video that said, 'This town, Glastonbury—it's like Greenwich, but half the price!'"

West of the river, a mere 10 miles away from Glastonbury, is West Hartford. An undercurrent of rivalry has long existed between West Hartford and Glastonbury, with both attracting Hartford's top earners from the healthcare, insurance, and education industries.

Although less than half the size of Glastonbury, West Hartford offers many of the same charms with its mix of idyllic small-town life and modern convenience.

Both towns are considered very walkable compared to the average Connecticut suburb, have highly rated public school systems, and have beautifully maintained their share of pre-1800s historic homes.

West Hartford, however, tends to be more expensive at its high end, standing at a median of $712,000 for its 06107 ZIP code, a slight dip from last year.

Robert Levine of ERA Real Estate, who lives and sells in West Hartford and the surrounding areas, says the two upscale suburbs have a few key differences.

Glastonbury has larger plot sizes, with homes often sitting on an acre or more of land, and has room to grow. West Hartford, a more suburban enclave with no real room left to build, has a denser, more bustling center of town.

"We're a destination. People come from 50 miles away to have dinner in our center," Levine says.

As for the metro being the hottest one in the country, the agent says he isn't surprised—he still sees multiple offers on turnkey homes that check all the boxes: good location, backyard, basement, two-car garage, etc.

But he declares that the area is in a "transitional market," with some homes sitting for several months.

"Homeowners are scratching their heads, like, 'Wait, my home won't sell in a weekend?'" he says.

"We're transitioning to what I call an 'equilibrium' market," he adds. "It's not necessarily favorable to either buyers or sellers. It's all about the property."

As for why central Connecticut keeps luring buyers, the agent notes the scenery, the small-town vibes combined with modern ease, and the tight-knit communities.

Kiri Blakeley writes about trending news at Realtor.com. She has also worked at Forbes Magazine, Forbes.com, CafeMom, and DailyMail.com, covering everything from billionaires to celebrities to crime. She lives in Brooklyn, and her cat foster Instagram account has over 4 million views.

#5586. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.

#5585. Texas AG narrows lawsuit against Epic, dropping claims over parental access settings

Texas AG narrows lawsuit against Epic, dropping claims over parental access settings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Texas is dropping a part of its lawsuit against Epic Systems, specifically the claims about how the company's software handles parental access to a child's electronic health records.

In December, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit against Epic, alleging that the health tech company monopolizes the electronic health record market and cements its dominance in the market through an "anticompetitive playbook."

The lawsuit, filed in Tarrant County District Court, also accused the company of engaging in deceptive practices that restrict parental access to their minor children’s medical records. On Tuesday, the Texas AG's office filed a notice of partial non-suit indicating it was dropping the deceptive practices claims against Epic.

The notice of partial non-suit states that the decision was made "in light of Epic’s recent changes to its software."

In previous statements, an Epic spokesperson said the company "does not determine parental access to children’s medical records."

"Decisions about parental access to children’s medical records are made by doctors and health systems, not by Epic," the spokesperson said.

The state is still moving forward with its antitrust claims under the Texas Free Enterprise and Antitrust Act. The Texas Attorney General's office alleges Epic "uses a wide range of exclusionary tactics to prevent potential competition from its partners, customers and even its own employees." According to the suit, these anticompetitive practices harm Texas hospitals and Texas patients by raising costs and blocking innovative technologies.

In the lawsuit, Paxton alleged that Epic "exploits its control" over patient medical records to automatically hide children’s medication lists, treatment notes and provider messages from parents when their child reaches 12 years old. Texas alleged that Epic’s default proxy-access configurations impede parents’ ability to see their children’s health information.

"These deceptive practices undermine the fundamental right of parents to direct their children’s healthcare" and violate Texas law, which grants parents complete and unrestricted access to their children’s medical records, the attorney general's office said in the lawsuit.

In a statement issued in December, Paxton referred to Epic as a "woke corporation" and stated that Epic's default proxy-access configurations "undermine the sacred rights of parents to protect and oversee their kids’ medical well-being."

In a statement provided to Fierce Healthcare on Wednesday, an Epic spokesperson said the Texas lawsuit includes "significant inaccuracies, including claims about MyChart's customer proxy settings."

"The state filed a voluntary dismissal of those claims on Tuesday. Ken Paxton's office requested that we change our customers' system settings. We said no because those decisions should be made by doctors and health systems and not by Epic. The lawsuit followed. The State should dismiss the remaining claims," the Epic spokesperson said.

In a Jan. 20 filing in Tarrant County District Court, the electronic health record giant said it makes "highly configurable software so that its customers, healthcare organizations across all fifty states, can determine what workflows and functionalities are needed to achieve their own compliance obligations—including with respect to parental access rights to medical records."

"What might be compliant in Texas might not be compliant in another state and vice versa, and those laws may change from time to time, as the law just did roughly four months ago in Texas. Configurability helps customers bridge that gap," the company wrote in its filing.

Epic said it would not "unilaterally go into each of its customers’ systems to change their individualized settings."

Epic also argued, in its court filing, that the state failed to produce facts or legitimate legal bases to support any of its claims. "When Epic asked the State to identify any Epic customers it claimed were not in compliance with the new law, the State did not identify a single Epic customer. What appears to be going on here is that the State has decided to target Epic over a politicized issue regarding proxy access that Epic does not belong in the middle of. The State confirms as much in its press release, calling Epic a 'woke corporation' that supposedly 'undermine[s]' parents’ rights," Epic wrote in its answer to the lawsuit.

In its Answer and Affirmative Defenses, Epic said that the state's antitrust claims against it are pre-textual and baseless. Epic denied Paxton's allegations of anticompetitive behavior, citing a lack of evidence and factual flaws in the lawsuit.

The case will carry over into a changing political landscape in Texas. Paxton, who launched the lawsuit, is leaving the Texas attorney general's office after more than a decade, after his unsuccessful bid for the U.S. Senate. Democrat Nathan Johnson defeated Republican Mayes Middleton in the Nov. 3 midterm election, becoming the first Democrat elected Texas attorney general since 1994.

The leadership change could bring a shift in the office's litigation priorities. Paxton's tenure was marked by high-profile legal battles over social and cultural issues, including transgender healthcare and parental rights.

Last year, the Texas Office of the Attorney General secured a settlement with Austin Diagnostic Clinic that required full restoration of parental proxy access for children aged 12 to 17. Paxton has also issued civil investigative demands to other EHR software providers over parental access to minor children's medical records.

The case will also have a new judge. Democrat Katherine Kim defeated Republican incumbent H. Dustin "Dusty" Fillmore III in the race for Tarrant County's 236th Judicial District Court.

#5584. Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success

For decades, explanations for why some children struggle with reading have often focused on two factors: intelligence and the ability to process visual information. Children who read easily have frequently been assumed to be more intelligent, while those who struggle have sometimes been viewed as less capable. Another common belief is that reading difficulties arise primarily from problems interpreting the words and letters on a page.

However, a major new study challenges these assumptions, suggesting that the abilities most important for reading success may be very different from what many people expect.

Dr. Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor in Texas A&M University's Department of Educational Psychology, led one of the most extensive investigations to date into how cognitive abilities relate to reading performance. The research brought together scientists from the University of Kansas, St. John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University to examine which mental skills best predict reading development and why some children encounter difficulties.

Massive Study Reveals What Really Predicts Reading Success

To investigate these relationships, the researchers combined 50,000 correlations drawn from 137 cognitive and achievement test batteries into a single statistical model. This large-scale approach allowed them to assess the contribution of individual mental abilities to reading performance while also helping clarify why previous studies had sometimes produced conflicting conclusions.

The findings revealed several surprises. Visual processing showed no meaningful relationship with reading ability across the analysis. General intelligence was associated with reading performance, but its influence was considerably smaller than some earlier research had suggested.

Instead, two less frequently discussed abilities emerged as particularly important predictors of reading success: auditory processing and comprehension-knowledge.

"One notable finding was that general intelligence was less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses," Hajovsky said. "Broad abilities such as comprehension-knowledge and auditory processing played strong, specific roles in reading beyond general intelligence, especially for decoding and comprehension."

Two Overlooked Skills Play a Major Role in Reading

Auditory processing involves recognizing and distinguishing the individual sounds that make up spoken words. For example, a child needs to identify the separate sounds within a word to understand how those sounds correspond to written letters. This skill helps support decoding, the process of working out how written words are pronounced.

Comprehension-knowledge refers to the vocabulary, concepts and background information a child has accumulated through learning and everyday experiences. Having this foundation makes it easier to understand the meaning of words, sentences and longer passages.

Together, these two abilities were more reliable predictors of reading performance than any other skills examined in the study. Other cognitive functions, including memory, reasoning and mental processing speed, also contributed to reading development, although they played more supporting roles.

The results suggest that reading is not simply a reflection of overall intelligence or how effectively a child processes visual information. Instead, it depends on several interconnected abilities, with language-related skills playing especially important roles.

What the Findings Mean for Children Who Struggle to Read

The research could help educators better understand why individual students experience reading difficulties. Rather than treating all reading problems as the same, teachers may be able to identify particular weaknesses and provide instruction that addresses those needs.

For families, the findings also offer an encouraging message. A child who has trouble reading is not necessarily less intelligent or incapable of becoming a strong reader. Difficulties may instead reflect specific abilities that need additional development and support.

"Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," Hajovsky said. "Struggles in reading are not a sign of low ability but often reflect one specific skill that needs strengthening within a larger system that works together."

The findings highlight the value of helping children build essential reading skills through consistent support, both in the classroom and at home.

According to Hajovsky, the most effective approach involves cooperation among schools, parents, and communities. Reading develops through a network of connected skills, and strengthening those foundations one step at a time can help children become more confident and capable readers.

#5582. Medical transport platform MedHaul, focused on high-needs patients, raises $4.1M

Medical transport platform MedHaul, focused on high-needs patients, raises $4.1M" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

MedHaul, a platform for coordinating medical transport, has raised $4.1 million in an unnamed round, Fierce Healthcare has learned exclusively.

The strategic round, which brings MedHaul’s total raised to date to $7 million, was led by Black Ops VC, with participation from Pier 70 Ventures, Seae Ventures, Stanford University, 450 Ventures (BCBS of Alabama), LaunchTN and American Cancer Society’s BrightEdge.

The latest capital will be used to expand deeper in oncology, which represents 60% of rides booked on the platform, and to support a forthcoming Epic integration.

Millions of Americans are affected by transportation barriers to care, and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services estimates that these barriers account for a quarter or more of missed clinic appointments. Missed appointments are associated with mortality among patients with chronic conditions and cost the system billions annually, according to one 2017 estimate.

MedHaul is a B2B platform working with providers and payers. Its tech helps providers match patients with medical transport according to acuity and accommodation needs, such as a wheelchair or stretcher. Care teams can use MedHaul to schedule and track transportation, with same-day and advanced bookings available. They can also manage billing, communicate with patients and identify those at greater risk of missing an appointment. MedHaul also rolled out a newer clinical trial product designed to support CROs and pharma clients.

The existing medical transport ecosystem is “very antiquated” and “heavily manual,” MedHaul founder and CEO Erica Plybeah told Fierce Healthcare. Many transport companies are small businesses that are not tech-savvy, or that need business development support. When MedHaul first entered the market, in 2019, some vendors didn’t even have a website or a social media page, Plybeah noted. And manual back-and-forths between care teams and ride providers means it can take upwards of two hours just to book a ride.

MedHaul’s network spans 17 states, primarily serving patients in the cancer, kidney disease, maternal health and behavioral health spaces. It also supports hospital discharges and rural patients. It has about 600 transport companies in its network.

MedHaul has also launched an enterprise platform, designed for large health systems and multi-location practices. Through a partnership with Uber Health, ride share and non-emergency medical transport bookings are available in one place, on the platform. The platform also provides real-time analytics into patient mobility, enabled by AI.

"There are opportunities in healthcare where AI is bridging the gap to solve for unmet needs—and that’s exactly what Erica and her team are doing at MedHaul,” James Norman, co-founder & managing partner at Black Ops VC, said in a statement. The user-friendly interface and focus on high-acuity communities “make MedHaul an attractive investment, and we’re proud to help them scale.”

Plybeah, who grew up in the Deep South with a grandmother who had diabetic and a double-leg amputee, saw how transportation issues affected her access to care. Throughout her career in clinical and research informatics, including at Epic Systems and St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, Plybeah “saw how transportation impacted institutions, when patients don’t show up on time, don’t show up at all, show up at the wrong facility … and it brought me back to being a little girl in the Mississippi Delta.”

Over half of MedHaul’s rides require mobility assistance, and 42% live in rural communities. MedHaul’s riders averaged eight rides per year in 2025.

Patients typically don’t pay anything for the rides booked on MedHaul. Instead, the MedHaul client—a provider or payer, for instance—sponsors the rides, often from an existing medical transport budget. In specialties with high transport volumes, providers may also use a patient’s benefit to find rides.

Same-day rides are available within 30 minutes to an hour, depending on acuity. For higher-acuity patients, a booking can take two to three hours, depending on the complexity of the transport required. MedHaul sees a 97% ride completion rate. Providers using MedHaul have reduced missed appointments by 25% and improved patient appointment timeliness by 52%, the company claims.

MedHaul has long used AI across its business. It has a conversational AI agent for older adults who prefer phone calls to texting. It also leverages AI agents to book rides within seconds for highly complex patients, and offers care teams MedHaul GPT, which they can use to ask questions about their programs and patients.

“We really prioritize good implementation,” Plybeah said, noting that there has been an explosion in digital health point solutions, but implementation is a whole different question. “We want this process to be as easy as possible for the end users.”

The company, which launched in 2019, is a public benefit corporation and a certified B Corp. While it’s still a for-profit business, its structure requires it to pursue a stated public benefit alongside financial returns. “We wanted our mission to extend beyond profit and to attract the right partners, investors, employees and customers who shared that commitment,” Plybeah said. “Our social mission is embedded in how we operate, build technology, serve patients and choose the people and organizations we work with.”

Plybeah is excited that there is more industry awareness of the social determinants of health. In the early MedHaul days, “folks seemed to think of transportation as a separate service,” she said. “And now I am grateful to see that folks are really considering transportation as part of the patient’s care journey, because it is.”

#5581. A New Wave of Opportunity Zones Is Coming in 2027—and Home Values Are Already Surging in Key States

The United States has thousands of new Opportunity Zones, a designation that could bring rising values to many emerging housing markets.

The Treasury Department last week announced 6,576 new Opportunity Zones (OZ), which will maintain that status for the next decade. All 50 states and the District of Columbia have zones in the mix, and 2,594 of them are in rural areas. OZs benefit from enhanced economic incentives, and they're targeted at communities with the potential to grow.

“By designating thousands of new Qualified Opportunity Zones, the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most," IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

This is the second round of OZs since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act established the program in 2017. The private sector has invested $110 billion in developing the first crop, Treasury said. The original OZs remain active through 2028, and the new ones begin in 2027. Some OZs were renewed.

States submitted nominations from about 25,300 census tracts eligible for the program, and leaders cheered their wins. There are about 25% fewer tracts than last time.

"Whether it's bringing new life to a downtown, creating great-paying jobs, or building housing for more families, these Opportunity Zones will help attract investments that can make a real difference in the lives of Ohioans," Gov. Mike DeWine said of Ohio's 260 new OZs.

“Virginia is ready to harness the potential of Opportunity Zones,” Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger said of the state's 153 new OZs. “I worked closely with local leaders across Virginia to make sure we supported the priorities that mattered most to local communities."

Property data group ATTOM analyzed 3,805 OZ census tracts from the last tranche and found median single-family home and condo prices rose in 48.1% them. Compare that to home prices outside of OZs, which rose 51.6%.

Some OZs see their home values rise much more quickly. ATTOM found that about 9.4% of the OZ census tracts saw their highest median home value since the Great Recession in the third quarter of 2026. About 27.1% of them saw double-digit growth in home values year over year.

“Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80% of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so, home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.”

As far as states with a lot of OZ price growth, Maine came in first, with 64% of its OZs seeing median home prices rise. South Carolina (61.3%), Wisconsin (58.3%), Virginia (53%), and Oregon (52.3%) rounded out the top five.

ATTOM noted that many of the census tracts recorded a low number of sales, so the data can be volatile. Still, 79.5% of them had home prices below the national median. Outside of them, just 50.4% of tracts had prices below the national median.

Michael Tillman, CEO of OZ developer PTM Partners, tells Realtor.com® the program also gives developers time to experiment. His company builds workforce housing in Florida using cold-formed steel and vertical integration.

"These are not build-and-flip products; we want to be there as their family grows," Tillman said of the units. "That's stickier than high-end luxury. There's got to be more institutional capital with that long-term focus."

OZs tend to have higher poverty rates, lower median family income, and more housing cost burdens than a typical area. Some are in urban areas, and others are in rural ones.

Brookings Institute analyzed the OZ program and found half of the zones saw "accelerated growth." But it said the designation alone doesn't create success. Local market conditions and state and local regulations play a role. And, while they do often mean new investment, that can vary depending on the development already there.

"Investment alone is not synonymous with shared prosperity," Brookings said in the report. "In some places, OZ capital has expanded housing supply, supported business formation, created jobs, and leveraged underutilized community assets—while in others, it flowed toward projects with limited community benefits or into neighborhoods already on a growth path."

Brookings also noted the first round of OZs came when the country already saw increased building. What this means in the current, challenged market has yet to be seen. States should develop a strategy for how to develop each zone.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5580. Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired

Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body, while the right side controls the left? This unusual arrangement is one of the most intriguing features of the nervous system, and scientists have proposed a new explanation that reaches back hundreds of millions of years.

Dr. Martin Wessendorf, a neuroscientist and associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota, studies how the brainstem regulates neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang specializes in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Together, they have examined the evolutionary origins of the brain's crossed connections.

In a study published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, the researchers explore several neural circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). Their hypothesis suggests that these connections may have developed because evolution built new brain circuits around an ancient visual system.

The brain contains numerous pathways that cross from one side of the central nervous system to the other. Understanding why these contralateral (midline-crossing) connections exist requires examining how different sensory and movement circuits developed over evolutionary time.

How the Brain Processes Visual Information

One possible explanation begins with the eyes. When light passes through the eye's lens, the image projected onto the retina is reversed. Objects appearing to our right are projected onto the left side of the retina, while objects on our left are projected onto the right.

Visual information travels along the optic nerve to a structure called the optic chiasm. Here, nerve fibers are organized so that information from the right visual field reaches the left side of the brain, while information from the left visual field is directed to the right side.

Some of these signals reach an ancient brain structure called the optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus). Located in the midbrain, this region helps produce fast reactions to visual events, such as suddenly noticing something moving nearby.

Each side of the optic tectum contains a representation of the opposite visual field. Deeper within the structure, information about physical sensations (somatosensory information) is also organized into corresponding maps.

Because the optic tectum exists in every vertebrate species, it is considered one of the most ancient structures in the vertebrate nervous system. Its early appearance may be especially important for understanding why so many other neural pathways cross sides.

Why Sensory Signals Cross the Brain and Spinal Cord

The researchers also examined two major pathways responsible for transmitting sensations from the body to the brain. Both cross the center of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be widespread among tetrapods (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians).

The first, called the dorsal column pathway, carries information about gentle touch, vibration, and the position of different body parts. Signals from the limbs and torso travel upward through the dorsal portion of the spinal cord before reaching another neuron in the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. From there, the pathway crosses to the opposite side.

Although fish lack this pathway, scientists have identified it in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Its presence across these major animal groups suggests that the arrangement emerged early in tetrapod evolution and has remained largely conserved.

The second pathway, known as the spinothalamic tract, transmits sensations involving pain, itching, and certain types of touch. Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord itself.

After crossing, signals travel upward to the thalamus, a brain region located above the midbrain that plays a central role in processing sensory and movement information.

This crossed arrangement is found in birds, mammals, and reptiles. It also occurs in some cartilaginous fish, including sharks and rays, suggesting that aspects of this organization have even deeper evolutionary roots.

How the Brain Controls Movement Across the Body

The crossed organization of the nervous system extends beyond sensation. The researchers identified three important pathways involved in controlling skeletal muscles that also connect one side of the brain with the opposite side of the spinal cord.

The first is the tectospinal pathway, which helps the body respond rapidly to information from the environment.

The optic tectum processes more than vision. It also receives information about sounds and physical sensations, organizing these signals into maps that align with its visual representation on the opposite side of the brain.

Imagine preparing to cross a street when you suddenly notice a car approaching from the corner of your eye. You instinctively turn toward the vehicle. The tectospinal pathway is one of the neural circuits that helps produce this rapid response. It can also coordinate similar reactions to unexpected sounds or touch.

The movement signals originate in the deepest layers of the optic tectum and travel through nerve fibers to the opposite side of the spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and certain cartilaginous fish.

Another important circuit is the rubrospinal pathway, which is thought to help animals control their limbs. It begins in a midbrain structure called the red nucleus and extends to the opposite side of the spinal cord. The pathway is especially prominent in most mammals, although it has also been identified in other tetrapods and some cartilaginous fish.

The Evolution of Fine Motor Control in Humans

The third pathway, called the corticospinal tract, has a particularly important role in humans because it supports precise movements, including the fine control of our fingers.

Its evolutionary history is more complicated than that of the other pathways.

All vertebrates possess a telencephalon, the forward portion of the brain that accounts for much of the brain's overall size in humans. However, only mammals have a cerebral cortex organized into six distinct layers.

This six-layered cortex supports sophisticated functions such as combining sensory information with memories, coordinating movement, and processing language.

The corticospinal pathway extends from the cerebral cortex toward the spinal cord, but its function varies among animals.

In most mammals, it primarily influences sensory processing. Nerve fibers reach spinal cord regions that receive information from the body, allowing the brain to regulate incoming sensations.

In primates (including humans) and certain other animals capable of highly precise movements, the pathway also reaches spinal cord regions responsible for controlling muscles. These connections make intricate actions possible, including the coordinated finger movements needed for delicate tasks.

Depending on the species, the corticospinal tract can regulate sensory information or contribute directly to movement. In either case, its fibers cross the midline of the nervous system.

The researchers suggest that humans may have developed advanced fine motor abilities by adapting an older neural circuit originally involved in controlling sensory input. Rather than creating an entirely new system, evolution may have given an existing pathway an additional purpose.

A 500-Million-Year-Old Explanation for the Brain's Crossed Wiring

Taken together, these neural pathways point toward a potentially surprising explanation for the brain's unusual organization.

The researchers propose that the earliest visual circuits helped establish a pattern in which sensory and movement pathways were organized across opposite sides of the nervous system. Later circuits may have inherited this arrangement as they evolved, particularly in tetrapods.

Because every living vertebrate possesses an optic chiasm and an optic tectum organized around information from the opposite visual field, the researchers suspect that these structures were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, approximately 538 to 486 million years ago.

If correct, this would mean that the basic organization underlying the brain's crossed connections began developing more than half a billion years before modern humans appeared.

The hypothesis may even be testable. Scientists could examine fossilized skulls from ancient jawless fish for anatomical evidence that might help establish whether these early animals possessed an optic chiasm and optic tectum.

An Evolutionary Inheritance Rather Than an Advantage?

The broader idea challenges the assumption that every unusual biological feature must have evolved because it provided a direct survival benefit.

Evolution often modifies structures that already exist instead of developing completely new systems. Once the ancient visual pathways established a crossed organization, that arrangement may have influenced how additional sensory and motor circuits developed.

In particular, the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have provided a structural foundation that later pathways followed.

Under this hypothesis, the brain's crossed connections did not necessarily arise because controlling the opposite side of the body was inherently more effective. Instead, they may reflect the lasting influence of an ancient arrangement that evolution repeatedly reused.

The result could be one of the most enduring examples of how the nervous system preserves its evolutionary history. The strange relationship between the brain's two hemispheres and the opposite sides of the body may ultimately trace back to the visual systems of animals that lived more than 500 million years ago.

#5578. Zus Health secures $33M to build the infrastructure for AI-powered clinical workflows

Zus Health secures $33M to build the infrastructure for AI-powered clinical workflows" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As healthcare companies race to build AI copilots and agents, startup Zus Health is betting that the bigger opportunity is creating the connected patient data layer those applications need to work reliably.

Zus Health, Jonathan Bush's health tech company, picked up $33 million in series B funding to build out the data foundation for healthcare AI. Drive Capital led the series B round. Sanofi Ventures, HealthX Ventures and Alumni Ventures, as well as existing investors Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), F-Prime, Maverick Ventures and JAZZ Venture Partners also backed the round.

The financing brings Zus's total capital raised to more than $100 million, and the fresh funding will support the company's continued investment in its intelligent patient record platform, national healthcare data network and AI-powered clinical workflows.

Zus has built its platform in three layers, according to Bush. The company first focused on building a nationwide patient record, a data network that pulls information into that record, and increasingly, AI-enabled workflows that automate care tasks using a more complete view of the patient.

Electronic health record systems (EHRs) succeeded at digitizing healthcare but failed to make patient information portable across organizations, Bush, founder and CEO of Zus Health, told Fierce Healthcare. Clinicians and care teams still spend valuable time searching for records and reconciling incomplete information. For patients, that can mean repeating their medical history at every appointment or relying on memory to recall past treatments. Advances in artificial intelligence now offer an opportunity to make healthcare information not just accessible, but actionable, according to Zus Health executives.

Launched in 2021, Zus Health developed what Bush calls an "always-on, FHIR-native, API-first medical record." It offers a shared health data platform designed to accelerate healthcare data interoperability by providing easy-to-use patient data at the point of care via a standalone app, API (application programming interface), embedded components and direct EHR integration. At the center of its approach is an intelligent, continuously updated patient record that serves as a shared foundation for healthcare applications.

The company's Zus Aggregated Profile (ZAP) brings fragmented clinical information together into a unified, longitudinal patient record, supported by AI-powered clinical intelligence that makes the information easier to use across applications and workflows, according to the company. The platform also has nationwide connectivity across EHR networks, pharmacy data, care event notifications, labs and other clinical data sources that continuously updates the patient record without requiring customers to build their own connectivity infrastructure.

"We're finally on to the last and critical piece of what I think the future of medical records looks like, which is standing up workflows that automate all of the tasks of patient care in a very bespoke way," Bush told Fierce Healthcare. "[Zus Health] developed the first data-rich networked medical record platform in the industry's history. Whether Zus wins or somebody else beats Zus at it, all electronic medical records in the future will be national."

He added, "And now, with AI, we have an extraordinary opportunity to build workflows that actually make delivering care easier, faster and more effective."

The company is betting that the next competitive player in healthcare AI will be the data infrastructure underneath the applications.

Zus Health, a Fierce 15 of 2025 honoree, wants to use its nationwide data network and longitudinal patient record as the infrastructure on which AI-powered clinical applications can run. The company's platform enables EHRs and other applications to work from a more complete, cross-provider view of the patient. Zus Health built AI solutions and flexible integration capabilities to put connected information to work across clinical and operational use cases, while enabling healthcare organizations to build applications tailored to their needs.

Zus works with value-based care organizations, digital health companies, provider organizations, as well as diagnostics and precision medicine companies. The company claims that in August alone its nationwide network supported more than 110 million networked transactions, while its AI-native clinical platform generated 39 million evidence citations year-to-date across its solutions—demonstrating both the scale of its connectivity and how patient information is being put to work across healthcare.

Zus supports solutions spanning pre-visit preparation, transitions of care, risk adjustment, quality gap closure and population health management. Its clinical intelligence capabilities, including AI-powered generated patient summaries (GPS), turn fragmented patient records into information care teams can use more efficiently and confidently.

The company plans to use the series B funding to build out its AI-powered clinical intelligence and capabilities and broaden its healthcare data network connectivity. Zus plans to expand its solutions to automate population health and care management workflows, while enabling customers and developers to create AI-powered workflows across value-based care, specialty care and other high-value use cases.

The company is seeing rapid growth in specialty care, particularly oncology, where complex patient records are spread across multiple providers. Zus' continuously updated, aggregated patient data enables more comprehensive and efficient reviews of treatment eligibility, clinical trial criteria and genetic testing—tasks that traditionally required extensive manual work by nurses and analysts using fragmented legacy EHR systems, Bush noted.

"We believe healthcare is entering a new era in which AI can fundamentally change how care is delivered, but that transformation depends on having reliable, connected patient information," said Molly Bonakdarpour, general partner at Drive Capital, in a statement. "Zus has built the foundation to address that challenge at scale. Its combination of technology, market opportunity and leadership gives us conviction in the company's ability to help shape the next generation of healthcare."

This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. #5576. Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn

Keeping daylight saving time in effect all year could bring brighter evenings, but new research suggests the change would come with a troubling consequence for American children. A nationwide switch could result in at least 2 billion additional trips to school in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks while reducing children's exposure to important morning sunlight.

The debate over permanent daylight saving time has gained momentum in Washington, D.C. This past summer, the U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation that would eliminate the annual return to standard time in the fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already approved measures supporting the change, which would take effect in those states if the federal bill becomes law.

The legislation remains stalled in the Senate, with school start times emerging as a major concern. Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would push sunrise an hour later during the winter months, leaving mornings darker from November through March. Although this would affect everyone traveling early in the day, researchers at the University of Washington wanted to understand what it would mean specifically for children heading to school.

Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Add Billions of Dark School Commutes

To measure the potential impact, the research team examined 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time measures. They combined school enrollment figures, individual school start times, and geographic coordinates to determine how frequently students would need to travel to school before sunrise. The researchers then calculated the total number of these trips under the proposed system and compared it with the current practice of changing clocks twice a year.

The results revealed substantial increases. In Washington state alone, permanent daylight saving time would produce nearly 35 million additional school commutes in darkness. Similar patterns emerged across the other 13 states, with Georgia showing the largest increase at approximately 71 million additional dark trips.

When the researchers extended their findings to estimate the nationwide impact, they calculated that permanent daylight saving time would create at least 2 billion more trips to school before sunrise compared with the current system.

The potential consequences go beyond inconvenient mornings. An analysis of U.S. traffic collision records found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely to occur during dark mornings as after sunrise. The findings were published October 29 in the journal Current Biology.

"It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology at the University of Washington. "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark."

Why Morning Sunlight Matters for Children's Health

Beyond concerns about traffic safety, losing access to morning sunlight could interfere with the body's natural daily rhythms. Bright light early in the day helps synchronize the circadian clock, the internal timing system that influences sleep, mood, appetite, and other important functions. When people receive too little morning light, maintaining these biological rhythms can become more difficult.

For children, who must typically follow fixed school schedules, darker mornings could mean missing a valuable opportunity to receive daylight at a time when their bodies need it.

"When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at the University of Washington. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."

The researchers also identified which communities would experience the greatest changes. Schools located near the western boundaries of time zones, including those in Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected because sunrise already occurs relatively late in those locations. Districts that begin classes early in the morning would face similarly large increases in dark commutes.

Mississippi and Alabama offer striking examples. Schools in both states begin, on average, before 8 a.m. Under the current clock system, each state has approximately 2 million school trips in darkness. With permanent daylight saving time, that figure would rise to more than 20 million trips per state.

"Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."

Why the 2 Billion Estimate May Be Too Low

Although the researchers used detailed school information to calculate changes in 14 states, their nationwide estimate required broader assumptions. To project what would happen if the entire United States adopted permanent daylight saving time, they assumed students would generally be leaving for school at around 8 a.m.

Because many children begin traveling earlier, the team believes the projected increase of approximately 2 billion dark commutes may substantially underestimate the actual impact.

"For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number."

The findings also raise questions about efforts to improve teenagers' sleep by delaying high school start times. Adolescents typically have biological clocks that shift later than those of younger children and adults, making later school schedules beneficial. The researchers argue that permanently moving clocks forward could undermine some of those gains by making morning sunlight less accessible.

One possible solution would be to start school later to compensate for the darker mornings. However, de la Iglesia argues that such a change could have ripple effects throughout daily life, potentially requiring families and workplaces to adjust their schedules as well.

"I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."

The researchers' findings highlight a central tradeoff in the debate over permanent daylight saving time. While eliminating seasonal clock changes would provide more evening sunlight during winter, the additional daylight would come at the expense of morning light, potentially affecting children's safety, sleep, and daily routines.

Additional study authors include high school student Daniel Zhang and University of Washington biology undergraduates Nirekh Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, and Micaela E. Romero.
