#5575. STAT+: Scientists debut map of basal ganglia, a key brain region involved in an array of diseases

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.

Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer.

#5574. CMS extends moratorium on new Medicare enrollments for hospice, home health agencies

CMS extends moratorium on new Medicare enrollments for hospice, home health agencies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration is extending its moratorium on new Medicare enrollments from hospice and home health agencies.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said Thursday that it will extend the moratorium by six more months as part of its efforts to combat fraud, waste and abuse in the Medicare program.

CMS said the initial moratorium window has allowed the agency "to conduct targeted investigations and deploy advanced data analytics" to identify potential cases of fraud. An extension was deemed necessary to continue that effort, as the "circumstances warranting the imposition of the moratoria have not yet abated."

The agency said that hospice and home health have long been considered high-risk areas for fraud.

“We’ve made real progress over the past six months, but fraud in hospice and home health persists and our work isn’t finished,” said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. “Medicare beneficiaries deserve protection from these bad actors, and American taxpayers need to know the programs they rely on aren’t being bled dry by fraudsters.”

Like the original moratorium, the extension applies nationwide. However, the extension will allow currently enrolled hospice providers or home health agencies to add new practice locations to their existing enrollment in Medicare. Providers currently enrolled in Medicare will not be impacted and can continue to provide services to beneficiaries.

The Trump administration has issued a six-month moratorium on hospice and home health agencies enrolling in Medicare as part of its efforts to combat fraud.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said in an announcement on Wednesday morning that the "data-driven" decision targets a key source of fraud activity. It follows a similar announcement made earlier this year of a moratorium on durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics and supplies companies.

During the six-month window, CMS said it will focus on identifying and investigating bad actors and deploying advanced analytics that help accelerate the removal of hospice and home health providers that are likely perpetrators of fraud.

CMS added that recent action under the broader White House fraud push has suspended payments to 773 hospice providers and 23 home health agencies in the Los Angeles area, totaling about $70 million in funds.

“We’ve seen systemic and deeply troubling fraud in the hospice and home health space, with bad actors exploiting some of our most vulnerable Medicare patients and stealing money from the American taxpayer,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in the agency's press release. “Today we’re shutting the door on fraud—preventing new bad actors from entering Medicare while we aggressively identify, investigate and remove those already exploiting them."

"This is about protecting patients, restoring integrity and safeguarding taxpayer dollars," Oz said.

CMS said that the moratorium will not affect providers currently enrolled in Medicare, and they can continue to offer key services to members. It will apply, however, to new applicants for participation and "certain changes in majority ownership," which CMS said can be used to "obscure control by bad actors."

The moratoria will also prevent suspected fraudsters from evading punishment by moving across state lines, CMS said.

The announcement, the agency said, builds on a number of steps CMS has taken of late to address fraud in hospice and home healthcare, including increased oversight in states with elevated risk of fraud, such as Arizona, California, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.

CMS is also conducting hospice site visits across the country to monitor operations and potentially identify suspicious behavior. In addition, it expanded a demonstration across several states—Florida, Illinois, Oklahoma, Ohio, North Carolina and Texas—that allowed for pre- and post-claim reviews of submissions from HHAs, which may stop improper payments before they're made.

The National Alliance for Care at Home, in a statement responding to the news, said it welcomes the administration's scrutiny and appreciates that "providers will still be able to conduct face-to-face recertification visits via telehealth during the enrollment moratorium, which will help avoid unnecessary care disruptions for patients and families." Still, it said the action raises concerns over access to care in high-demand areas and urged CMS to focus its efforts on "high-fraud markets" or actors without catching the rest of the sector in its net.

“CMS must use data-driven, risk-based program integrity measures and focus resources on boots-on-the-ground surveys and enforcement of existing oversight mechanisms that root out the blatantly bad actors without potentially limiting patient access to care or punishing high-quality providers operating in good faith," Alliance CEO Jennifer Sheets said in the statement.

#5573. AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage

Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects.

The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss.

Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans.

"The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism."

The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments.

Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression.

BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature, has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD.

How Artificial Intelligence Uncovered a Hidden Molecule

Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult.

Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function.

A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments.

Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process.

The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them.

One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use.

AI Searches 20,000 Human Genes for New Hormones

To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts.

The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites.

These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical.

"The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity.

The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes.

A Tiny Peptide Produces a Surprising Result

GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells.

One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls.

The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals.

Food Intake Drops by Up to 50% in Animal Experiments

The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle.

The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger.

The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams.

Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.

Together, the findings suggest that BRP may influence both appetite and metabolic health, although it remains unknown whether people would experience comparable benefits.

Could BRP Avoid Common Ozempic Side Effects?

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is the possibility that BRP could provide weight loss benefits while avoiding some unwanted effects associated with semaglutide and similar medications.

To investigate potential side effects, the researchers monitored the behavior and physical responses of the treated mice and pigs. They found no significant differences in movement, water consumption, anxiety-related behavior, or fecal output compared with control animals.

The absence of changes in fecal production was particularly interesting because constipation is a known side effect of medications such as Ozempic. The experiments also showed that BRP promoted fat loss without the substantial muscle loss that can accompany some weight reduction treatments.

Nausea is another common concern with existing GLP-1 medications, although animal experiments cannot fully establish whether BRP would prevent that symptom in people. Human testing will be essential to determine the molecule's actual side effect profile.

Additional investigations into brain activity and other physiological responses reinforced the idea that BRP works differently from semaglutide. The peptide activated distinct neuronal and metabolic pathways rather than simply copying the effects of GLP-1.

This difference may explain why the researchers observed strong appetite suppression without several of the behavioral and digestive changes they were monitoring.

What Comes Next for the Potential Ozempic Alternative?

Despite the encouraging findings, BRP is still at an early stage of development. Researchers need to understand more about exactly how the molecule communicates with cells and how its effects might be sustained over longer periods.

One priority is identifying the cell surface receptors that recognize BRP. Receptors are specialized proteins that respond to particular chemical signals, allowing cells to detect messages and trigger appropriate biological responses. Determining which receptors BRP activates could help explain its effects on hunger and metabolism.

The team also wants to investigate ways of extending the molecule's activity inside the body. Peptides can be broken down relatively quickly, potentially requiring frequent injections. A longer-lasting version of BRP could make treatment more convenient if it eventually proves effective in people.

The ultimate challenge will be establishing whether its apparent advantages in animals translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Clinical trials will need to evaluate its safety, effectiveness, appropriate dosage, and potential side effects before it could become a practical obesity treatment.

"The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades," Svensson said. "Nothing we've tested before has compared to semaglutide's ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans."

Scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Minnesota; and the University of British Columbia also participated in the research.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK125260, P30DK116074, K99AR081618 and GM113854), the SPARK Translational Research Program at Stanford, Stanford Bio-X, the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the American Heart Association, a Stanford Medicine Dean's Fellowship Award, the Carlsberg Foundation, and the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance.

Svensson and Coassolo are named inventors on patents involving the use of BRP peptides to treat metabolic disorders. Svensson is also a cofounder of Merrifield Therapeutics.

#5571. Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel

Scientists have developed a new gel that could make it possible to regrow damaged tooth enamel, potentially overcoming one of the biggest limitations in dental care. Unlike bones and many other tissues in the body, tooth enamel cannot naturally regenerate once it has been lost. The new treatment offers a promising way to rebuild this protective layer, strengthen teeth, and help prevent future decay.

The innovation comes from researchers at the University of Nottingham's School of Pharmacy and Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering. Their new material is inspired by the biological processes that form tooth enamel during early childhood. It is designed to repair enamel that has been weakened by mineral loss or worn away by erosion, while also reinforcing enamel that remains healthy.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, could pave the way for a new generation of dental treatments that go beyond protecting existing enamel and actually help restore its structure.

One of the most promising features of the technology is its simplicity. Dentists could apply the gel directly to teeth using a procedure similar to existing fluoride treatments, making it potentially easy to incorporate into routine dental care.

Unlike conventional fluoride products, however, the new gel contains no fluoride. Instead, it uses a material made from proteins that imitates important characteristics of the natural proteins responsible for guiding enamel formation when teeth first develop.

Once applied, the gel forms a thin but durable coating that penetrates the tooth's surface and fills microscopic cracks and gaps. This coating then provides a framework for rebuilding the mineral structure of enamel.

The process relies on calcium and phosphate ions, two essential mineral components naturally present in saliva. The gel attracts these minerals and helps organize them into new crystals that grow in an orderly pattern.

Scientists call this process epitaxial mineralization. Essentially, it means that new mineral crystals grow in alignment with the existing enamel, allowing the newly formed material to become structurally integrated with the original tooth surface.

This organization is especially important because enamel gets its exceptional hardness and durability from the precise arrangement of its mineral crystals. Simply depositing minerals on a tooth is not enough to recreate the complex structure that makes natural enamel so effective.

By guiding crystal growth, the new gel can restore both the microscopic architecture and the physical properties of healthy enamel.

A Potential Solution for Tooth Sensitivity and Decay

The researchers also discovered that their material can be used on exposed dentine, commonly called dentin in the United States. Dentin is the layer of tooth tissue beneath the enamel. It is softer than enamel and contains tiny channels that can transmit sensations toward the nerves inside the tooth.

When enamel wears away, or gums recede, exposed dentin can make teeth particularly sensitive to hot, cold, sweet, or acidic foods and drinks.

The new gel can encourage the formation of an enamel-like mineral layer over exposed dentin. This could help reduce tooth sensitivity while also improving the attachment of dental restorations, such as fillings and other treatments used to repair damaged teeth.

The potential benefits are significant. Enamel deterioration is a major factor in tooth decay and contributes to dental problems that affect nearly half of the world's population. These conditions can cause pain, infections, and eventually tooth loss. Poor oral health is also associated with broader health problems, including diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

One of the greatest challenges in dentistry is that enamel has no living cells capable of rebuilding it after teeth have fully developed. Although saliva can naturally replace some minerals lost during the earliest stages of enamel damage, the body cannot regenerate substantial amounts of enamel that have been worn away.

Existing treatments, including fluoride varnishes and remineralization products, can help protect teeth and repair early mineral loss. However, they cannot fully reconstruct enamel that has already been lost.

The new technology aims to overcome that limitation by encouraging the formation of new mineral tissue with properties resembling those of the original enamel.

Regenerated Enamel Performs Like Natural Tooth Enamel

The research team tested the mechanical strength and durability of the regenerated material under conditions designed to mimic everyday use.

These experiments examined how the newly formed enamel responded to activities and exposures that teeth routinely experience, including brushing, chewing, and contact with acidic foods.

The results were encouraging. According to the researchers, the regenerated enamel displayed mechanical properties comparable to those of healthy natural enamel, suggesting that the material could provide more than a temporary protective coating.

Dr. Abshar Hasan, a postdoctoral fellow and the study's lead author, explained why recreating enamel's internal structure is so important.

"Dental enamel has a unique structure, which gives enamel its remarkable properties that protect our teeth throughout life against physical, chemical, and thermal insults. When our material is applied to demineralized or eroded enamel, or exposed dentine, the material promotes the growth of crystals in an integrated and organized manner, recovering the architecture of our natural healthy enamel. We have tested the mechanical properties of these regenerated tissues under conditions simulating 'real-life situations' such as tooth brushing, chewing, and exposure to acidic foods, and found that the regenerated enamel behaves just like healthy enamel."

These findings suggest that the gel could eventually offer a way to restore the strength and protective function of damaged enamel rather than simply slowing further deterioration. However, the laboratory results do not yet establish how well the treatment will perform over extended periods in patients.

Beyond its ability to regenerate enamel, the researchers emphasize that the technology was developed with practical dental applications in mind.

The gel is designed to be safe, simple to apply, and suitable for manufacturing on a larger scale. Its versatility could also allow it to be incorporated into several types of dental products, potentially benefiting patients of different ages with enamel erosion, tooth sensitivity, or other problems involving exposed dentin.

Professor Alvaro Mata, Chair in Biomedical Engineering & Biomaterials at the University of Nottingham, led the study and highlighted the potential for translating the discovery into products that dentists can use.

"We are very excited because the technology has been designed with the clinician and patient in mind. It is safe, can be easily and rapidly applied, and it is scalable. Also, the technology is versatile, which opens the opportunity to be translated into multiple types of products to help patients of all ages suffering from a variety of dental problems associated with loss of enamel and exposed dentine. We have started this process with our start-up company Mintech-Bio and hope to have a first product out by next year; this innovation could soon be helping patients worldwide."

The researchers have already begun working toward commercialization through their company, Mintech-Bio, with the goal of introducing an initial product as early as the year following the announcement.

Although further development and clinical validation will be important before the technology becomes an established dental treatment, its ability to recreate the structure and strength of natural enamel represents a promising advance.

If the approach proves successful in patients, it could fundamentally change how dentists address enamel loss, opening the possibility of rebuilding tooth surfaces that previously could only be protected or restored using conventional dental materials.

#5570. Inside the $3.25 Million Pasadena Glass Pavilion That’s Still Studied in Architecture Classes Today

A three-bedroom midcentury modern home designed by Case Study architect Craig Ellwood has just come on the market in Pasadena, CA, for $3.25 million. It features a notable cantilevered glass pavilion.

Built in 1965, the Kubly House was originally constructed for less than $45,000. The 2,227-square-foot home has since been thoughtfully updated.

“What makes this house special is its architecture and design, and how true it has remained to the original,” says Chris Suarez, who is co-listing the property with Kimberly Benz of Suarez + Benz at Compass. “Nothing was significantly altered. Everything done was intended to restore the house to its original condition. The footprint, the floors, the glass—everything has remained true to the original design.”

Located in the Linda Vista neighborhood, the home has an iconic redwood, cantilevered glass pavilion that opens to a single-level floor plan. The private half-acre lot includes a pool and spa surrounded by lush landscaping with eucalyptus and oak trees.

With exposed post-and-beam construction, clean horizontal lines, and expansive walls of glass, the home was designed to give the illusion of floating above its natural surroundings. The deck was recently restored using specially milled wood.

“It was sourced from northern Washington and brought down here,” Suarez notes. “Everything was done painstakingly to avoid altering the house’s integrity, architecture, and design. That being said, significant work has been done, including updates to the roof, infrastructure, air conditioning, and electrical systems. All the major systems have been updated, but you wouldn’t necessarily know it because the work was done so carefully.”

Originally commissioned by ArtCenter College of Design alumni and educators Don and Sally Kubly, the home represents their understanding of design and the culture of the college community. It is still studied in classes there.

“Don was ArtCenter’s first president in Pasadena,” Suarez explains. “There’s also a connection through Craig Ellwood, who designed ArtCenter’s main campus building. The main campus is an incredible steel-and-glass building designed by Ellwood. Don played a significant role in moving the school from Los Angeles to Pasadena, where he served as president for many years. He’s very well known within that community, and this house is significant to the college’s history and culture.”

Based on available architectural records, the Kubly House is said to be Ellwood’s only documented residential project in Pasadena.

After remaining in the Kubly family for nearly six decades, the home changed hands for $3.6 million in 2022. Since then, the sellers have undertaken a preservation-minded restoration with Carl Bronson of Bronstruction, updating major systems to contemporary standards.

“A house that helped usher in much midcentury modernism was the Glass House, designed by Philip Johnson around 1948 or 1949,” Benz notes. “That design was definitely something Ellwood loved. You can clearly see that house’s influence here, which is important because it reveals some of the influences behind Ellwood’s work.”

Benz adds that the home’s design was also influenced by Ellwood’s peers, including midcentury designer George Nelson.

“A furniture plan developed for the house clearly referenced Mies van der Rohe and George Nelson, both important figures in midcentury modern design,” she says. “Even the deck and the steps leading to the house resemble a George Nelson bench. There’s actually a bench built into the concrete wall near the pool that resembles a George Nelson design. I don’t know whether Nelson designed or made it, but the influence is certainly there.”

The house is special because many of the original details have remained intact, she adds.

“You can see the influence of the people Ellwood admired throughout the house,” Benz says. “That significance is what makes this house important when you look at the midcentury modernist movement. All these examples are visible in the house and remain there.”

Some of the built-in furniture has a distinctive style, too.

“There’s a stunning floating credenza that looks like a George Nelson piece,” she notes. “We think it might be one of his designs. It’s in the living room. There’s also a built-in console that might be a George Nelson design as well. So, some of the furniture is actually built into the architecture.”

While some pieces are originals and others are reproductions, Benz says, “the most important thing was following the original plan. The history of this house is everything.”

When staging the home, she says they were “fortunate to discover an original interior design study among the blueprints, plans, and documents that came with the house. We were able to look at that study, and it became a guide and a road map for staging the property. Sourcing the furniture was a challenge because we had to find the specific pieces.”

The city of Pasadena has also identified the property as eligible for individual listing on the National Register of Historic Places.

Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. As a writer and editor, she has worked for a variety of online and print publications, including Inked magazine, Jetset, Westchester magazine, JustLuxe, The Boston Globe, and U.S. Veterans Magazine. #5569. UnitedHealth releases independent audit of its medical policy development practices

UnitedHealth releases independent audit of its medical policy development practices" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Over the past year, UnitedHealth Group has conducted a series of independent reviews of its practices as part of a broader turnaround effort at the company.

The healthcare giant released the last of these analyses on Thursday, digging into the processes it uses to establish medical policies. The reviews were conducted by FTI Consulting and Rubrum Advising, a provider-led firm with expertise in medical coverage policies.

While the auditors dove into the processes the insurer uses to develop its medical policies, the report doesn't examine the application of those polices and any impact on coverage denials, an area where UnitedHealthcare has drawn significant public scrutiny.

The report concluded the company's methods "were strong overall and that the medical policy development process reflected numerous best practices."

For instance, UnitedHealthcare's Medical Policy team uses a structured and standardized process to establish medical policies, rooted in evidence-based and stakeholder-informed approaches. Clinical evidence comes from nationally recognized authorities, and epidemiologists play a key role in the review process, per the report.

In addition, the analysts concluded that the team is well-staffed with qualified workers and operates under a strong governance model. Medical policies are built "using systematic evidence review, evidence-based tools and industry best practices," and UnitedHealthcare is transparent about posting these policies and making updates.

All policies are reviewed at least once per year, the report found.

CEO Stephen Hemsley said in a letter to investors that the company will continue to conduct such analyses.

"We will continue to subject key practices across UnitedHealth Group to independent review, share results publicly and make changes where needed," Hemsley wrote. "This work reflects our broader commitment to transparency, accountability and continuous improvement."

While the report concluded that overall processes in place at UnitedHealth were up to snuff, the consultants did offer multiple areas of improvement for the company, too. For instance, the analysts said that the team could improve its documentation practices, including how it details criteria for policy development.

Plus, the report suggests that UnitedHealthcare review how it documents vetting criteria for internal and external subject matter experts. The company could also do more to formally document training and education for members of its governance committee.

Medical policy documents can be lengthy and complex, so the consultants recommended the insurer consider developing a template that standardizes the written format for each policy, which would make it easier to understand. For example, the template could make it easier to connect the evidence summary to the coverage rationale.

"While these gaps do not diminish the overall strength of the program, addressing them would further enhance transparency and consistency and provide opportunities for continued refinement," the analysts wrote.

#5568. Across the U.S., homegrown experiments aim to save kids from their phones

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Isabella is a chronic disease reporter writing about how the Trump administration is tackling the nation’s health epidemic — or not. You can reach her on Signal at isabellacueto.03.

MILWAUKEE — Kat Zilka sat on the floor of her living room, beside a glowing Christmas tree and a pile of essays, and felt like weeping. It was late in 2022, and she had asked her 12th grade digital journalism students to reflect on their relationships to devices.

“The things they were writing were deeply disturbing,” she said.

Teenagers quietly enduring online abuse, using their phones all night without their parents’ knowledge, or trapped in a cycle of deleting and redownloading social media. Their words made real what Zilka had been observing for years — how the light in students’ eyes was dimmer, especially since Covid — and revealed the astonishing magnitude of the problem.

“It was like they were just waiting for someone to ask,” she said.

That semester would change the trajectory of Zilka’s career, and place her at the forefront of an emerging national conversation about kids’ degrading attention, and its effect on their health. At that time, there were no surgeon general advisories on the matter, nor were there dozens of state legislatures clamoring to crack down on phones. It was people like Zilka, on the ground, trying to beat back an encroaching mental health crisis with minimal guidance.

Over winter break, she sketched out an elective course called “Digital Detox.” Students loved the class, she said, in part because Digital Detox was unlike anything else they were doing in school. That began with the first 10 minutes of class, when students would just sit with their thoughts. “Halfway through the semester, they were, like, hankering for it,” Zilka said.

Despite the mostly positive feedback, she felt the course was bound by an unresolved tension: It was adding to the academic pressure, while trying to help students’ mental health.

The students didn’t want more coursework. They wanted a support group.

Zilka thought something spiritually connected to Alcoholics Anonymous, or even the church youth groups of her childhood, could fit the bill. “The opposite of addiction is connection,” she said. Elsewhere in the country, other grassroots experiments began to take shape — all molded by youth, and fueled by a sense of urgency that was absent from mainstream politics and the slow crawl of science.

“Young people are developing today. They don’t really have time for us to wait 10 years to find out how to help them,” Rachel Hanebutt, a Georgetown University researcher studying teens’ relationship to tech, said.

As regulators and researchers, already years behind on the problem, struggle to respond to ever-evolving platforms, homegrown efforts have a distinct advantage, she said: They are nimble.

Some projects teach young people to set hard boundaries with social media, and use rich experiences IRL to draw them away from digital isolation. Others are blatantly political, aiming to turn teenagers’ rebellious streaks on Big Tech itself.

Their collective mission is to give generations of American kids raised with an iPad and schooled with a Chromebook an escape hatch — out of the disorienting blue haze and into the rushing, cool air of the real world.

Zilka was so convinced by what she saw in Digital Detox that she formed a nonprofit, called dis//connect, and quit her teaching job. The first meeting took place in May 2024.

She also raised a small pot of money, around $1,200. About a year ago, Zilka brought in clinical psychologist Thekla Ross, a leader in the emerging field of “digital harm reduction,” to measure how well the program is working and find ways to expand the model.

Now, on most Monday and Thursday nights, Zilka and Ross gather with about 8 high schoolers in their respective meetings. The hourlong sessions start by logging average daily screen time by hand and slipping silenced phones into a filing box. Then they celebrate the “slow media” they’re consuming, and sit quietly for 10 minutes.

Spread across the tables are a variety of fidget toys, coloring books, and word searches so the teens have something to do with their hands. They talk about what’s on their minds: Friend breakups, frustrating teachers, and toning themselves down in public because someone might be recording (a habit Zilka and Ross dub, in a forthcoming book, “flatlining”).

Caroline, an ambitious rower with a darting gaze and mouthful of braces, is nervous about not making the team for an upcoming tournament in Boston. By Thursday night, she’d made the boat, and was troubled by other ideas.

Tonight’s reading, from Anna Lembke’s “Dopamine Nation,” is about how the author became obsessed with romance novels — a parallel to how social media hijacks the brain’s reward system. Like Lembke, Caroline has recently struggled to read anything but love stories.

“I didn’t even think about it until now,” she said, noting how short she is of her goal of 150 books for the year.

A copy of “To Kill a Mockingbird” sat on her shelf for weeks, and went back to the library untouched, as she devoured romance stories instead. The harder something is for the brain, the more delayed the reward, Zilka acknowledged.

“It can be really hard in our world to convince ourselves to do the delayed gratification thing,” she says.

It all reminds Caroline of a recent discussion in her literature class, about how books have changed as fewer people read for pleasure. She and Tala, a curly-haired friend who’s new to the group, commiserate over the lack of fellow bookworms at school.

Their male counterparts are even less likely to read for fun — or, it seems, come to groups like these. Boys at school are gripped instead by the mind-altering influence of Clavicular and online gambling, the girls say.

(Earlier in the night, a polite overachiever named Ethan said attending dis//connect eased his anxiety about feeling left out on apps like Snapchat. Now less self-conscious, he goes out of his way to wish classmates “happy birthday” to their face. Recently, a girl responded by saying he could’ve texted her instead.)

Boys and girls tend to use the internet about the same amount — four in 10 U.S. teens say they are online almost constantly, according to a 2025 Pew survey of 13-to-17-year-olds. However, boys face different pressures online, such as the meteoric rise of sports betting apps, which experts say build on the alluring design elements of other platforms.

“Convince me that Kalshi, predictive markets, FanDuel, and DraftKings are not social media companies,” said Hanebutt, the Georgetown researcher.

Betting apps could further obscure the nature of digital addiction, who is most vulnerable to harm, and why.

As it is, we don’t really know what phones are doing to us.

Type the words “phone addiction” into a search bar on social media, and you will find a long and seamless scroll of hundreds of videos on the topic.

It might be a surprise, then, to read credible researchers’ disagreements about whether the word “addiction” is the right term for what’s happening. Some, like the prominent Digital Mental Health Group at the University of Cambridge, question whether social media shares the same underlying neurocognitive mechanisms as addictive substances.

But other researchers say the “infinite scroll” and algorithmic feeds are addictive by design, and that heavy users can experience addiction-like symptoms: craving, withdrawal, quitting attempts, and relapse.

“It’s akin to each time you smoke a cigarette, the cigarette itself increasing in nicotine content to you in particular,” said Vikram Bhargava, an assistant professor at the George Washington University business school who studies the ethics of technological innovations.

(Meta, as part of its historic $17.1 billion settlement with dozens of states, agreed to interrupt endless scrolling and add time limits to teen Instagram accounts. The company has denied that its products are addictive.)

The questions don’t stop there. Over a decade after the birth of Instagram, researchers aren’t even sure about whether social media causes mental distress. It might just be feeding into vulnerable people’s underlying problems. Or, it could be doing both. Two people, given the same platform for 30 minutes, can have vastly different experiences.

“It might not be the dose of use — how many hours an adolescent uses social media — but actually the nature of that use,” Kelila Kahane, a psychiatrist and fellow in child and adolescent psychiatry at NewYork-Presbyterian, said.

This is the technological maze researchers find themselves in as they confront the fact that the kids are not alright. Kostadin Kushlev, leader of the Happy Tech Lab at Georgetown University, is one of the people grappling with these unknowns.

His lab received a grant from the National Institute of Mental Health to study how social media directly affects teens’ mental health. The study involves giving a group of 10-to-14-year-olds their first phone. For three months, half the group has as much access to social media as their parents allow, while the other half has none. All of the kids complete brief daily surveys, along with three longer surveys, over the course of six months.

The phones also track their movement, sleep, and online activity, such as most-used apps and what times of day participants are opening them.

“That sort of addresses a second critical issue in the literature: A lot of the evidence is based on these very basic, rudimentary, almost laughable measures of screen time,” Kushlev said. One common metric asks: On a spectrum of “not at all” to “several times per day,” how often did you use your phone in the past week?

Tech companies are still the keepers of the richest datasets, which could actually help researchers tease out differences between users. But in the U.S., the companies are not required to share that information with outside scientists. Most of what we know about the depths of data extraction has come from Silicon Valley whistleblowers, he said.

“It’s so stark when you think about it,” Kushlev said. Researchers spend years designing studies and applying for grants, only to spend bucketloads of money for data that’s less useful than what tech companies already have.

That lackluster data is then driving policy.

“All we have is these negative correlations, and it’s sort of like, ‘Oh, I guess it’s bad, so let’s ban it all,’” he said.

Dozens of states have enacted phone restrictions in recent years, and the Trump administration has encouraged others to pursue “bell-to-bell bans.” Congress too has floated screen time-related bills, including a recent bipartisan proposal that would limit social media use for those under 16.

Evidence is mixed on how well bans work. In Australia, where in 2024 lawmakers banned kids under 16 from making accounts on certain social media platforms, initial data suggest little changed about teens’ reported use.

In some cases, in-school restrictions have been shown to reduce phone usage in class, or marginally improve academic performance in certain subjects. But they can also lead to more disciplinary action or even declines in school performance at the start of the policies. Data are still unclear on whether they provide any long-term mental health benefits.

While it’s too soon to tell what really works, a recent review by the Cambridge group found promising evidence for things that add friction — think: a pause or prompt before opening a certain app — and programs that teach practical digital skills. Teacher- or peer-led sessions focused on attention and self-control also demonstrated some short-term benefit.

“The underlying mechanisms of change may be more important than the intervention level itself,” they wrote.

People leading attention projects intuit something else: Simply taking screens away won’t solve the nation’s problems. Teens need something new to be excited about.

Consider a bright September day on Brooklyn’s picturesque Washington Street, where tourists are weaving around each other, necks craned, snapping pictures of the Manhattan Bridge, its enormous crown poking between historic buildings.

Here, all of a sudden, are a half-dozen teenagers bisecting the cobblestone street, arms lifted, hands assuming the claw shape of a smartphone holder, but grasping only air.

For five minutes, the small band of “attention scholars” does this: Pretends to take pictures of the bridge while surrounded by people trying to take actual pictures of the bridge. After a few minutes, their presence becomes a human barricade, then an attraction — cameras click at them, people stare and giggle. Others frown.

One woman, clad in a sunhat, tries to fill the claw-shaped void with her own cellphone, wordlessly requesting that one of the teens take a picture of her against the backdrop.

Then Jahony Germosen, who has been standing nearby with a timer, rings a bell and the teens file back into the lobby of their building, where they erupt into giddy laughter.

That was a “public intervention” done by “attention activists” training at the Strother School of Radical Attention.

SORA, as insiders call it, is perhaps the best-known group in the U.S. devoted to this kind of work. Started by academics and artists in 2023, it operates as a nexus for a movement that seeks to liberate people’s minds from Big Tech.

“You can think of this as a health problem. You can think of this as a productivity problem. We’re thinking of it as a systemic problem,” Peter Schmidt, SORA’s program director, told STAT. “You need collective action.”

Its weeklong summer camp, now in its third year, introduces young people to the idea of attention as political, and something worth defending. “Our attention is the precondition for our freedom,” Schmidt said.

Some of the campers have never been on social media. They feel that gives them a clearer vision of their peers’ dependence. (STAT agreed to identify participants only by age.)

One participant, a 14-year-old science fiction lover, wasn’t allowed to have a cellphone until seventh grade — later than most American kids — and felt routinely excluded from conversations because of it. SORA camp has been refreshing, she said. “It helps that other people are noticing the same thing.”

The 17-year-old sitting beside her, wearing thick eyeliner and armfuls of beaded bracelets, recently stumbled upon the New York City Luddites, an anti-smartphone group that hosts events around the city.

She found the idea of “human fracking” — SORA’s teaching that tech companies are forcibly breaking, capturing, and selling human attention — particularly compelling, since she already disliked the fossil fuel industry.

The 17-year-old started hating how she felt when she’d mindlessly scroll TikTok and Pinterest, so she deleted the apps. In her free time, she’s learning how to hand-code a website. And she tries to talk to her parents instead of scrolling before school. Sometimes, they are the problem.

Another 14-year-old, sporty and shy in a black hoodie, was forced by his dad to come to the camp, but has found some of the discussions thought-provoking. That may be as far as it goes.

When he called a friend to share what he’d been up to at the end of August — turning off his phone, staring at a sculpture with childlike wonder, talking about extractive profit models — his friend scoffed, “What the hell is that?”

There was more to it: Together, the teens identified the New York City subway as a site of human fracking, because so many people are scrolling during their commute. The students identified “questions to live with” — What would my life be like as a fish? How long would it take to swim to Manhattan from here? — instead of consulting artificial intelligence chatbots. They’ve also delved into “Attensity!” the movement’s manifesto, published this year.

Camper Consuelo “Leo” Burnett, 17, is well acquainted with this world because her father, the Princeton history professor D. Graham Burnett, is one of SORA’s founders. Nevertheless, she has grown personally invested in the subject of attention, and acts as an idea translator for younger students. (STAT obtained permission to use Burnett’s full name.)

During the Covid pandemic, Leo Burnett lived in an extended lockdown, barely leaving home for over a year as her family tried to protect two immunocompromised members. She got her first cellphone around the same time. “The internet was my one way of feeling connected with the world,” she said, her blue eyes wide.

But she was also prone to anxiety and panic attacks throughout childhood, and in her search for queer community, joined online groups where mental illness was seen as a “badge of honor,” Burnett said. Her mental health cratered, and she developed an eating disorder.

This complicated history with social media started to make more sense once Burnett went to SORA camp. Her reliance on TikTok for bursts of dopamine no longer felt like a personal failing.

“It’s a multibillion dollar industry trying to control young people’s attention,” she said.

There is a view of the attention crisis that deems it a runaway train.

But the other take — the one adopted by many who work with youth, and who must hold onto some optimism to get through the day — is that we have more control than we think.

“Attention spans have not, in some deep, permanent way, been hampered,” Michael Vazquez, associate director of UNC Chapel Hill’s Parr Center for Ethics, said.

Vazquez and his colleagues have undertaken one of the largest academic efforts so far to test that idea. Last year, they received an almost $800,000 grant to run a three-year experiment, “Educating for the Virtues of Attention,” or EVA.

Attention is a virtue because it’s “upstream of a lot of other things we care about,” such as learning, flourishing, and building relationships, Vazquez said.

As part of EVA, every freshman at Chapel Hill is exposed to curriculum about the demands on our attention, and how those pressures shape our well-being. Some students are finding courses gone totally analog: Instead of submitting assignments on a web portal, they are told to write them in a physical journal. Or, a professor might add extra hoops to jump through before a student can use technology in class.

The idea is to give all students a taste of EVA, “and then we have deep dive opportunities for those who want to continue,” he said. That could look like an oral reading of ancient poetry at a local bookshop, or it could be a phone-free picnic in the university’s arboretum.

This fall, a cohort of over two dozen undergraduates committed to restricting their social media use to a certain number of hours per week as part of a new program called “Carolina Unplugged.” They gather weekly for dinner to reflect on their progress and plan cultural events on campus.

Each student received a Brick, a physical device that disables select apps once a person taps their phone to it. Apps remain blocked until the phone is tapped again. The freebie was what initially drew in Natalie Easley, a 20-year-old junior from Bethesda, Md. She had tried all of the built-in tools for controlling screen time, but nothing worked.

Since middle school, Easley had deleted apps and then caved, redownloading them. How many times had she gone through that cycle? “This is not even exaggerating: Probably like 50-plus,” she said.

But within days of leaving home with her phone Brick’d — and not being able to undo it until the evening — she realized how much better she felt. “I didn’t even realize how much of a compulsion it was, just to pick up my phone,” said Easley, a math and philosophy double major. Then she started to notice how many people walked around with their heads down, scrolling between classes. Her evenings spent on X were no longer satisfying.

“Twitter is fake. My phone is fake. Why is something that is not tangible ruining my day or making me pissed off?” she said.

She deleted X and Instagram, and slashed her average daily screen time by one-third, down to four hours. Easley has found that, free from social media, she can use her phone for discrete tasks — to take photos, learn about things she’s interested in, or text her friends.

She also has more time to let her mind wander. On a recent day, it summoned Aristotle’s assertion: We are what we do.

If one-third of her waking hours were spent online, Easley realized, “then maybe I am, like, my phone.”

“When you’re not distracted, you’re actually able to think about it.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated the year dis//connect meetings began.

#5567. A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves

Muscles can begin losing their strength and ability to recover surprisingly early in the aging process. Over time, muscle tissue may develop scar tissue, accumulate fat, and lose some of the specialized fibers responsible for rapid, powerful movements. These changes can make everyday activities more difficult and gradually reduce mobility and physical independence.

Now, scientists in Japan have identified a promising molecule that could help protect the body's natural muscle repair system and potentially make it more effective. In laboratory experiments, the compound strengthened an important biological signal involved in muscle regeneration, increasing its ability to connect with a key cellular receptor by more than twofold.

The discovery comes from a team led by Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi at Kyushu University's Faculty of Agriculture. Their findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest a possible new approach to addressing the cellular changes that make aging muscles increasingly difficult to repair.

How Aging Disrupts the Body's Muscle Repair System

Skeletal muscles are the muscles attached to bones that allow us to walk, lift objects, maintain posture, and perform other voluntary movements. Although these muscles experience wear and tear throughout life, they also have a remarkable ability to repair themselves.

Much of that repair depends on specialized stem cells known as satellite cells. These cells normally remain inactive, positioned alongside muscle fibers until they receive a signal that repair or regeneration is needed. Once activated, they can multiply and develop into muscle cells that help restore damaged tissue.

An essential part of this process involves a protein called hepatocyte growth factor, or HGF. Despite its name, HGF plays important roles beyond the liver, including helping activate the stem cells responsible for muscle regeneration.

Under normal conditions, HGF is stored within the supportive material surrounding muscle fibers. When muscles experience an injury or mechanical stimulation, such as physical movement or stretching, the protein can be released.

HGF then attaches to a receptor called c-met on the surface of satellite cells. Receptors are specialized proteins that receive molecular signals and trigger responses inside cells. In this case, the interaction helps awaken dormant satellite cells, allowing them to multiply, mature, and participate in repairing muscle fibers.

But this carefully coordinated system becomes less reliable with age.

A Hidden Chemical Change May Weaken Aging Muscles

The researchers' previous work revealed that HGF can undergo a chemical modification known as nitration. This process attaches a chemical group called a nitro group to particular locations on a protein, potentially changing its structure and interfering with its normal activity.

For HGF, the researchers identified two especially important locations, Y198 and Y250. Both lie within the region involved in attaching to the c-met receptor.

When these sites undergo nitration, HGF becomes less capable of connecting with its receptor. The result is similar to a key that has become damaged and can no longer operate its intended lock.

This disruption could have important consequences for aging muscles. Even if the body continues producing HGF, chemical changes may prevent the protein from properly activating the stem cells needed for tissue repair. The researchers believe this mechanism may contribute to age-related muscle wasting and declining regenerative capacity.

"HGF is not necessarily missing as we age," explains Tatsumi. "Rather, it can be chemically altered after it is made. That led us to wonder whether a compound with strong antioxidant capacity might protect HGF, either by preventing nitration or by compensating for the functional loss it causes."

Scientists Test Two Powerful Sulfur Compounds

To investigate that possibility, the team studied two compounds with strong antioxidant properties: glutathione trisulfide (GSSSG) and lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS).

Antioxidants can help limit certain types of chemical damage caused by reactive molecules. Such damage can interfere with proteins and other essential components of cells, particularly when the body's normal protective systems become less effective.

The two compounds belong to a chemical family called trisulfides. Their defining feature is a chain of three sulfur atoms connected to one another. This arrangement gives them unusual chemical properties, including an ability to participate in reactions involving the transfer of electrons, known as redox reactions.

Because these reactions play important roles in cellular chemistry, trisulfides have attracted growing interest as potential ingredients in new medicines.

In the first set of experiments, both compounds reduced nitration at the two vulnerable sites on HGF. However, preventing this chemical modification did not completely restore the protein's ability to attach to c-met.

The scientists therefore increased the amount of trisulfide used relative to HGF. They changed the molar ratio, which compares the number of molecules of each substance, from 1:4000 to 1:8000.

That adjustment produced an unexpected result.

An Unexpected Discovery Creates "Super HGF"

At the higher concentration, LASSS did much more than protect HGF from chemical damage. It also dramatically improved the protein's ability to bind to its receptor.

Compared with untreated HGF, the protein exposed to LASSS showed more than twice the binding affinity for c-met. In other words, it could attach to its target receptor much more strongly, potentially enhancing a critical step in the muscle repair process.

The treatment also made HGF more resistant to the loss of function caused by nitration, particularly at the Y198 site.

Notably, the effect was specific to LASSS. Although GSSSG had also reduced nitration in the earlier experiments, it did not produce the same improvement in receptor binding.

"This exceeded our expectations," comments Tatsumi. "We knew trisulfides had diverse biological functions, but we never expected that simply mixing HGF with LASSS would produce such a striking effect.

"What this tells us is that LASSS does more than simply neutralize reactive molecules. It may interact directly with HGF and induce a subtle structural change, creating an enhanced 'Super HGF' form that binds c-met more strongly and resists nitration."

The researchers suspect that LASSS interacts with HGF in a way that slightly alters the protein's three-dimensional shape. Because a protein's shape helps determine how well it interacts with other molecules, even a small structural adjustment could substantially change its activity.

The result is what the team describes as "Super HGF," a potentially enhanced form of the body's existing muscle repair signal.

Importantly, stronger receptor binding does not automatically establish that muscle regeneration itself has improved. Additional experiments will be needed to determine whether this molecular enhancement translates into better muscle healing and strength.

Mouse Experiments Reveal Promising Protection

After observing the effects in laboratory experiments, the researchers wanted to determine whether LASSS could also protect HGF inside living muscle tissue.

They used mice subjected to tail suspension, an established experimental method for studying muscle atrophy. By reducing normal weight bearing and muscle use, this technique produces some of the changes associated with prolonged inactivity, including muscle deterioration.

Mice that received LASSS before the experiment showed significantly less HGF nitration than untreated animals. This suggested that the compound's ability to protect the muscle repair protein was not limited to controlled laboratory conditions.

Once again, GSSSG failed to produce the same protective result.

These findings provide early evidence that LASSS can influence the chemical processes affecting HGF within living animals. However, the mouse experiments demonstrated protection against nitration, not that LASSS restored lost muscle mass or improved physical strength.

The researchers emphasize that studies involving aging animals are still necessary to establish the compound's effectiveness and safety in vivo, meaning within a living organism.

A Potential New Strategy Against Age-Related Muscle Loss

The discovery could eventually contribute to treatments aimed at maintaining muscle function during aging or extended periods of inactivity.

Muscle deterioration is not limited to older adults. It can also occur during prolonged bed rest or other situations in which muscles are used less frequently. When muscle repair mechanisms become impaired, recovering lost strength and function can become especially challenging.

Rather than replacing the body's natural repair machinery, the approach explored in this study seeks to protect and enhance an existing biological signal. If the benefits can be confirmed in future studies, strengthening HGF activity could become one strategy for supporting muscle regeneration.

The scientists also believe that the underlying effects of LASSS on HGF may extend across species. That raises the possibility of applications not only in human medicine but also in veterinary care, particularly for aging companion animals such as dogs and cats.

For now, the findings represent an early step toward understanding how a naturally occurring muscle repair pathway might be strengthened. Whether LASSS can safely and effectively preserve muscle function during aging remains an open question.

Still, the unexpected discovery that a sulfur-based compound can both protect and enhance a critical repair protein offers a promising direction for future research, with the long-term goal of helping people maintain mobility, independence, and a better quality of life as they grow older.

Weekly Rundown: Ohio State Wexner, Microsoft ink tech deal; OpenEvidence launches free Access Intelligence tools" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Nov. 9 to 13.

Revenue management company R1 expanded Thursday its revenue operating system Phare OS with six connected AI solutions to bring agentic automation across pre- and post-bill healthcare operations

Four of the tools are now commercially available: Phare Auth, Phare Audit, Phare UM and a new Phare Denials module. Meanwhile, executives say Phare CDI and Phare Recovery are in early access with select customers—with broader availability expected in 2027.

“We’ve established Phare OS as the foundation for a different model of revenue management where technology isn’t measured by how many tasks it automates, but by the results it delivers,” said Joe Flanagan, R1 CEO, in a statement. “After decades of helping providers navigate the complexity of [the] revenue cycle, we know what it takes to improve performance. We’re bringing that expertise together with AI and payer intelligence, and we stand behind the outcomes. This is the level of accountability health systems should expect from their revenue management partners.”

OpenEvidence announced Wednesday the launch of Access Intelligence, a slate of tools built directly into its platform that allows clinicians to access affordability and coverage information.

Access Intelligence is free to all clinicians and can answer questions about availability and eligibility on more than 2,500 patient support programs, like copay savings and patient assistance, the company says. Other key features include:

The company says the suite will “continue to evolve to best support clinicians through the complex affordability and coverage landscape.”

“Programs exist to help patients with treatment access, and prior authorizations can be won, but the process is so fragmented and time-consuming that engaging with it is nearly impossible,” said Ania Bilski, M.D., OpenEvidence clinical AI vice president, in a statement. “Access Intelligence is our commitment to helping physicians and patients close the loop of care, from identifying support programs to completing enrollment to getting a prior authorization approved. Choosing the right treatment should be the hard part. Getting the patient access to it shouldn’t be.”

The Ohio State University and Microsoft announced Tuesday a five-year strategic partnership that aims to accelerate innovation across clinical care settings, education and research.

“Artificial intelligence represents one of the most significant opportunities to transform and improve how hospitals care for patients,” said John Warner, M.D., Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center CEO, in a statement. “Through this collaboration, we have an opportunity to help reimagine the future of healthcare as we bring together Ohio State’s academic medical expertise with Microsoft’s technological capabilities to accelerate the pace of innovation across patient care, research and education.”

Microsoft and the Ohio State Wexner Medical Center are co-developing a smart hospital model through the partnership, while also modernizing clinical and research applications and workloads through the cloud, unifying data and using AI to support care teams.

The American Medical Association (AMA) adopted a policy on Monday that declares AI can be used to aid physicians and assist with clinical tasks, but cannot be granted licensure, professional titles or certifications to practice medicine.

Moreover, the organization said it will advocate for legislation that establishes a framework for physician oversight of AI clinical-decision making. The organization also is calling for protections for physicians when AI tools cause patient harm.

AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., said in a statement that "patients deserve to know who is responsible for their care."

"Physicians also need the authority, oversight and liability protections to make independent decisions when AI is part of the care team," Underwood said.

Identity verification company Clear launched Monday two integrations within the Epic Toolbox, which will allow health systems to verify outside providers and prescribing clinicians.

The company’s CLEAR1 identity platform is now available through Epic Toolbox for EpicCare Link and electronic prescribing of controlled substances. The prescribing integration is available in Epic’s End User Authentication category.

“Doctors and nurses shouldn't spend their shifts proving who they are,” said David Bardan, CLEAR SVP, general manager and head of healthcare, in a statement. “Getting into a patient's chart and prescribing a controlled medication are two more places they no longer have to start from scratch. We're using secure identity to make healthcare safer and easier for care teams, from the first day to the first patient, and every shift after.”

Ellipsis Health, a voice AI care management company, acquired Kouper Health, a startup that built AI agents deeply embedded in clinical workflows.

Kouper's AI agents work inside health system electronic health record (EHR) systems like Athenahealth and Epic to coordinate care from scheduling through discharge and follow-up.

The deal pairs Ellipsis's "emotionally intelligent" AI voice care manager, Sage, with Kouper's native EHR integrations and longitudinal patient maps to deliver continuous, connected patient care, according to the companies.

Ellipsis Health works with seven of the top 20 health plans in the U.S. and leading academic medical centers and integrated delivery networks.

Founded in 2022, Kouper has raised funding from investors including CVS Health Ventures, General Catalyst and 25madison. Its technology embeds AI agents into health system workflows and builds longitudinal patient maps that bring information from across a patient’s care into a more unified view. Ellipsis' Sage can pick up from there with discharge follow-ups, medication adherence support and clinical check-ins by phone and text. Sage is used by nine of the top 15 U.S. health plans and has delivered up to 7x ROI for customers, the company said.

Sage is powered by a patented "empathy engine" trained on over 3 million labeled clinical conversations. It analyzes vocal cues in real time to assess emotional signals and adapt its interactions. Through phone and text, Sage supports care management tasks including enrollment, clinical assessments, medication adherence and post-discharge follow-up.

Kouper’s team is joining Ellipsis. Both companies will continue serving existing customers under their respective brands while developing a combined product roadmap, with new offerings for health systems expected in the months ahead.

“Healthcare has enormous potential to benefit from AI, but the hard part has been making that technology work for patients and care teams,” said Mainul Mondal, founder and CEO of Ellipsis Health, in a statement. “We have extraordinary clinicians, but we can’t solve access and continuity problems by asking them to do more. Kouper brings critical infrastructure for making that possible inside health systems. By combining their native integrations and longitudinal patient maps with Sage’s emotional intelligence, we can help care teams extend their reach and deliver more continuous, personalized support.”

#5563. A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease

A natural substance found in broccoli could offer an unexpected new approach to treating a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system. Researchers at Swinburne University have identified promising effects from the compound, raising hopes for a more affordable and accessible treatment for patients with few available options.

The disease, known as Friedreich ataxia, causes nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord to gradually deteriorate. As the damage progresses, patients lose their ability to coordinate movements, walk, and speak. The condition can also shorten life expectancy, and there is currently no cure. Approximately 200 Australians are living with the disease.

In a new study, scientists found that sulforaphane, a naturally occurring compound in broccoli, can increase levels of frataxin, a protein that is present in insufficient amounts in people with Friedreich ataxia. The researchers also found that the compound can help protect vulnerable nerve cells from damage.

How a Broccoli Compound Could Protect Nerve Cells

Frataxin plays an important role in keeping cells functioning properly, particularly those with high energy demands, such as nerve cells. In Friedreich ataxia, a genetic defect leads to reduced production of this essential protein, contributing to the progressive damage that characterizes the disease.

Sulforaphane appears promising because its potential benefits extend beyond increasing frataxin levels. Research indicates that it can also influence several biological processes involved in disease progression, including cellular stress and inflammation. Addressing multiple sources of damage at once could make the compound a valuable candidate for further investigation.

The findings are particularly encouraging for children with Friedreich ataxia. According to lead researcher Associate Professor Faith Kwa of Swinburne University, children account for a large proportion of those affected, yet no treatments specifically approved for pediatric patients are currently available.

"Friedreich ataxia is a devastating rare genetic disease that progressively steals a child's ability to walk, speak, play, and ultimately survive," she says.

"This novel therapeutic agent can target the underlying cause of the disease, while delivering an affordable and accessible therapy worldwide, improving treatment opportunities for families affected by this life-limiting disease.

"This discovery brings us closer to a future where children with Friedreich ataxia experience a better quality of life, greater independence, and an improved chance of long-term survival."

A Potential Treatment That Could Be More Accessible

One of the most encouraging aspects of sulforaphane is that it is not an entirely unfamiliar substance. The compound already has an established safety record in both children and adults, and purified, biologically active forms are commercially available.

These advantages could make it easier to develop a widely accessible treatment if future clinical trials confirm that sulforaphane is effective against Friedreich ataxia. However, further research is essential before scientists can determine whether the promising findings will translate into meaningful benefits for patients.

Kwa explains that the rarity of Friedreich ataxia creates additional challenges for researchers. Because relatively few people have the disease, public awareness is limited, making it more difficult to attract the funding needed to investigate potential treatments.

Researchers Seek Funding for Clinical Trials

The Swinburne team hopes to secure financial support for clinical trials that would examine whether sulforaphane can deliver the same promising effects in people living with the disease.

"We are hoping to gain funding to conduct clinical trials and further prove the positive impact the broccoli compound could have on those suffering from Friedreich ataxia," she says.

"Sulforaphane already has an established safety record in children and adults, and its pure and bioactive form is commercially available. This means if clinical trials prove successful, its rollout could accelerate the path to patient impact."

For patients and families facing a progressive illness with no cure, even improvements in everyday functioning and independence could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their work will not only advance treatment possibilities but also bring greater attention to a condition that remains largely unknown to the public.

"Even if we can raise awareness of this debilitating condition or improve one person's quality of life, our efforts will have been worth it."
